before.answer: No meer Man since the Fall, is able in this Life, perfectly to keep the Commandments of God, but doth daily break them, in Thought, Word, and Deed.
before.right: No mere man since the fall is able to keep God's commandments perfectly.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:1695_bap.note: Sin brings God's curse now (Galatians 3:10: those under the law are under a curse), His wrath coming (Ephesians 5:6), and eternal fire to come (Matthew 25:41).

before.question: What does every sin deserve?
before.answer: Every sin deserves God's wrath and curse, both in this life and in the life to come.
before.right: God's wrath and curse, both in this life and in the life to come

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:1695_bap.note: Acts 20:21 states repentance toward God and faith in the Lord Jesus; Isaiah 55:3 and Proverbs 8:34 call people to listen, come, and wait diligently, which teaches the use of the means.

before.question: What does God require of us, that we may escape His wrath and curse, due to us for sin?
before.answer: To escape the wrath and curse of God due to us for sin, God requires of us faith in Jesus Christ, repentance unto life, with the diligent use of all the outward means by which Christ communicates to us the benefits of redemption.
before.right: Faith in Jesus Christ, repentance unto life, and diligent use of means.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:1695_bap.note: Acts 11:18 names repentance unto life as God's gift to the Gentiles; Ezekiel 36:31 shows loathing of sin, Isaiah 1:16-17 shows turning from evil to doing right, and Joel 2:13 shows God's grace and compassion.

before.question: What is Repentance unto Life?
before.answer: Repentance unto Life is a saving Grace, whereby a Sinner, out of a true Sense of his Sin, and Apprehension of the Mercy of God in Christ, doth, with grief and hatred of his Sin, turn from it unto God, with full Purpose of, and Endeavor after, new Obedience.
before.right: A saving grace from sense of sin and God's mercy turning to God.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:1695_bap.note: Matthew 28:19-20 names baptism and teaching; Acts 2:42 names the apostles' teaching, the breaking of bread, and prayer. The claim that these means convey redemption's benefits to the elect is confessional teaching, not stated here.

before.question: What are the outward and ordinary Means, whereby Christ communicateth to us the Benefits of Redemption?
before.answer: The outward and ordinary Means, whereby Christ communicateth to us the Benefits of Redemption, are his Ordinances, especially the Word, Baptism, the Lord's Supper, and Prayer; all which Means are made effectual to the Elect for Salvation.
before.right: His ordinances, especially the Word, Baptism, the Lord's Supper, and Prayer.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:1695_bap.note: The gospel comes with power in the Holy Spirit (1 Thess 1:5), opens eyes to turn to God (Acts 26:18), and the word of God's grace builds believers up (Acts 20:32).

before.question: How is the Word made effectual to Salvation?
before.answer: The Spirit of God maketh the Reading, but especially the Preaching of the Word, an effectual Means of convincing and converting Sinners; and of building them up in Holiness and Comfort through Faith unto Salvation.
before.right: The Spirit maketh the Preaching of God's Word an effectual Means of convincing and converting Sinners unto Salvation

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:1695_bap.note: Watching daily at wisdom's doors (Prov 8:34) and asking God to open our eyes (Ps 119:18) show diligence and prayer; faith (Heb 4:2), love of the truth (2 Thess 2:10), hiding the word in the heart (Ps 119:11), and doing it (Jas 1:25) cover the rest.

before.question: How is the Word to be read and heard, that it may become effectual to Salvation?
before.answer: That the Word may become effectual to Salvation, we must attend thereunto with Diligence, Preparation, and Prayer; receive it with Faith and Love, lay it up in our Hearts, and practice it in our Lives.
before.right: Attend with diligence and prayer, receive with faith and love, practice in our lives.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:1695_bap.note: Paul says neither planter nor waterer is anything but God gives the growth; baptism saves through Christ's resurrection, not the water; Christ baptizes with the Spirit; faith receives it. The Supper is not addressed by these verses.

before.question: How do Baptism and the Lord's Supper, become effectual Means of Salvation?
before.answer: Baptism and the Lord's Supper become effectual Means of Salvation, not for any Virtue in them, or in him that doth administer them, but only by the Blessing of Christ, and the working of the Spirit in those that by Faith received them.
before.right: Not from virtue in them or the minister, but by Christ's blessing.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:1695_bap.note: Christ commands baptizing (Matt 28:19); baptism pictures union with Christ in His death, burial, and resurrection and new life (Rom 6:3-5); it puts us into Christ (Gal 3:27); it is for forgiveness of sins (Acts 2:38).

before.question: What is Baptism?
before.answer: Baptism is an Ordinance of the New Testament instituted by Jesus Christ, to be unto the Party baptised, a Sign of his Fellowship with him, in his Death, Burial, and Resurrection; of his being ingrafted into him; of Remission of Sins; and of his giving up himself unto God through Jesus Christ, to live and walk in newness of Life.
before.right: New Testament ordinance instituted by Christ signifying fellowship in death and life.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:1695_bap.note: Peter tells those who heard the gospel to repent and be baptized, and Mark says whoever believes and is baptized will be saved. Baptism follows repentance and faith; obedience is only implied, via Matthew 28:20.

before.question: To whom is Baptism to be administered?
before.answer: Baptism is to be administered to all those, who actually profess Repentance toward God, Faith in, and Obedience to our Lord Jesus Christ, and to none other.
before.right: To all who actually profess repentance toward God and faith in Christ.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Psalm 100:3 says outright, "It is He who made us, and we are His," so the answer God is stated. Genesis 1:27 supports it by recording that God created man.

before.question: Who made you?

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Psalm 139:7-10 says no place escapes God's presence: heaven, Sheol, the farthest sea. Jeremiah 23:24 agrees that He fills heaven and earth.

before.question: Where is God?

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Exodus 20:16 forbids bearing false witness against a neighbor, so the commandment teaches truthfulness; the answer, "to tell the truth," is the positive form of that prohibition.

before.question: What does the ninth commandment teach us?

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Romans 3:20 says the law brings awareness of sin, and Galatians 3:24 says it leads us to Christ. Together they teach both our duty and our need of a Saviour.

before.question: Of what use are the ten commandments to us?
before.answer: They teach us our duty, and show our need of a Saviour.
before.right: They teach us our duty, and show our need of a Saviour.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Philippians 4:6 tells believers to present their requests to God in prayer, and John 16:23 promises that whatever they ask the Father in Jesus' name, He will give. Together they teach the answer.

before.question: What is prayer?
before.answer: Prayer is asking God for things which he has promised to give.
before.right: Prayer is asking God for things which he has promised to give.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Jesus says, "this is how you should pray," then gives the prayer, so the Lord's Prayer is the pattern He gave for teaching us to pray.

before.question: What has Christ given us to teach us how to pray?

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Counting the requests in Matthew 6:9-13 gives six: hallowed be Your name, Your kingdom come, Your will be done, daily bread, forgiveness of debts, and not leading into temptation or delivering from evil.

before.question: How many petitions are there in the Lord's Prayer?

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: John 1:18 says no one has ever seen God. Hebrews 4:13 says nothing in creation is hidden from God's sight, so he sees everything, including us.

before.question: Can you see God?
before.answer: No; I cannot see God, but he always sees me.
before.right: No; I cannot see God, but he always sees me.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Matthew 6:10 asks for God's kingdom to come and His will to be done on earth; Matthew 24:14 calls the gospel of the kingdom the message to be preached in all the world.

before.question: What do we pray for in the second petition?
before.answer: That the gospel may be preached in all the world, and believed and obeyed by us and all men.
before.right: That the gospel may be preached in all the world and believed and obeyed by all

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: 1 John 3:20 says God "knows all things," and Hebrews 4:13 says nothing in all creation is hidden from His sight, which matches the answer's "nothing can be hid from God."

before.question: Does God know all things?
before.answer: Yes; nothing can be hid from God.
before.right: Yes; nothing can be hid from God.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: No shown verse numbers the sacraments. The count of two (baptism and the Lord's Supper) comes from church teaching; Ephesians 4:5 mentions one baptism but does not count sacraments.

before.question: How many sacraments are there?

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Jesus commands baptism in Matthew 28:19, and 1 Corinthians 11:23-25 says the Lord Jesus took bread and cup and told the church to do this in remembrance of Him.

before.question: Who appointed these sacraments?

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: None of the shown verses mention sacraments or state their purpose. Acts 14:22 and 2 Corinthians 1:5 speak of strengthening and comfort generally, so the answer comes from church teaching on the sacraments.

before.question: Why did Christ appoint these sacraments?
before.answer: To distinguish his disciples from the world, and to comfort and strengthen them.
before.right: To distinguish his disciples from the world, and to comfort and strengthen them.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: 1 Peter 3:21 says that "this water symbolizes the baptism that now saves you," and Acts 8:38 shows Philip baptizing the eunuch by going down into the water.

before.question: What sign is used in baptism?

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Those who embraced the message were baptized, and in Samaria people who believed Philip's preaching of the gospel were baptized, both men and women. Belief comes before baptism.

before.question: Who are to be baptized?

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Job 42:2 says God can do all things and no plan of His can be thwarted; Psalm 115:3 says He does as He pleases. The answer's "holy will" wording is a reasonable reading of these.

before.question: Can God do all things?
before.answer: Yes; God can do all his holy will.
before.right: Yes; God can do all his holy will.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Children are brought to Jesus so He can place His hands on them and pray for them, and He calls them to Himself, saying the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these.

before.question: Does Christ care for little children?
before.answer: Yes; for he says, "Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these."
before.right: Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them, for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Romans 6:3-4 says those baptized into Christ were baptized into His death and buried with Him, so that they may walk in newness of life. The answer follows as a plain teaching from this.

before.question: To what does your baptism bind you?
before.answer: To be a true follower of Christ.
before.right: To be a true follower of Christ.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Jesus says of the bread, "This is My body, which is for you," and he broke it. "For our sins" is not in this verse; forgiveness of sins is linked to the cup in Matthew 26:28.

before.question: What does the bread represent?
before.answer: The body of Christ, broken for our sins.
before.right: The body of Christ, broken for our sins.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Paul says the cup is the new covenant in Christ's blood (1 Cor 11:25), and Matthew 26:28 says that blood is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.

before.question: What does the wine represent?
before.answer: The blood of Christ, shed for our salvation.
before.right: The blood of Christ, shed for our salvation.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Paul requires each person to examine himself before eating the bread and drinking the cup, and 1 John 3:23 names belief in Christ and love for others as God's commandment. Repentance is not named for the Supper.

before.question: Who should partake of the Lord's Supper?
before.answer: Only those who repent of their sins, believe in Christ for salvation, and love their fellow-men.
before.right: Only those who repent, believe in Christ for salvation, and love their fellow-men

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Paul says Christ was buried and then raised on the third day, so the answer follows: he did not stay in the tomb but rose on the third day.

before.question: Did Christ remain in the tomb after his crucifixion?
before.answer: No; he rose from the tomb on the third day after his death.
before.right: No, he rose from the tomb on the third day

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Hebrews 9:24 says Christ entered heaven itself to appear on our behalf before God, and Hebrews 7:25 says He always lives to intercede for those who draw near to God through Him.

before.question: Where is Christ now?

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Matthew 25:31-32 says the Son of Man comes in His glory and gathers all nations before His throne to separate them. John 12:48 places the judgment by Christ's words on the last day.

before.question: Will he come again?
before.answer: Yes; at the last day Christ will come to judge the world.
before.right: Yes; at the last day Christ will come to judge the world.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Paul says all Scripture is God-breathed and useful for training in righteousness, so that the man of God is equipped for every good work. The answer follows from these verses.
creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.doubt: The verses say Scripture trains in righteousness and equips for good works, but they do not say "alone," which goes slightly beyond the text.

before.question: Where do you learn how to love and obey God?

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Ecclesiastes 12:7 says the dust returns to the ground and the spirit returns to God who gave it. "World of spirits" is the catechism's wording for where the spirit goes, drawn from that verse.

before.question: What becomes of men at death?
before.answer: The body returns to dust, and the soul goes into the world of spirits.
before.right: The body returns to dust, the soul enters the world of spirits

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: 1 Corinthians 15:52 says that at the last trumpet "the dead will be raised imperishable," which is the answer quoted. Isaiah 26:19 and 1 Corinthians 15:42 also speak of the dead rising.

before.question: Will the bodies of the dead be raised to life again?
before.answer: Yes; 'the trumpet will sound, the dead will be raised imperishable.'
before.right: Yes; 'the trumpet will sound, the dead will be raised imperishable.'

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Revelation 14:10-11 describes torment in fire and sulfur with smoke rising forever, and Revelation 20:10 places the tormented in the lake of fire, giving the place, torment, and endlessness.

before.question: What is hell?
before.answer: A place of dreadful and endless torment.
before.right: A place of dreadful and endless torment.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Jesus says He is preparing a place in His Father's house and will come back to welcome His people so they may be where He is, which teaches that the righteous are taken to heaven.

before.question: What will become of the righteous?
before.answer: They shall be taken to heaven.
before.right: They shall be taken to heaven.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Paul says believers "will always be with the Lord" (1 Thess 4:17), and David says God fills him with joy in His presence with eternal pleasures (Ps 16:11). Together they teach the answer's happy, forever-with-the-Lord heaven; "glorious" is not stated.

before.question: What is heaven?
before.answer: A glorious and happy place, where the righteous shall be forever with the LORD.
before.right: A glorious and happy place where the righteous shall be forever with the LORD

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Genesis 4:1 says Adam had relations with his wife Eve and she bore Cain. Genesis 3:20 names Eve as the mother of all the living, so Adam and Eve are the first parents.

before.question: Who were our first parents?

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Genesis 2:7 says the LORD God formed the man from the dust of the ground, and Genesis 2:22 says He made the woman from the rib taken from the man.

before.question: Of what were our first parents made?
before.answer: God made the body of Adam out of the ground, and formed Eve from the body of Adam.
before.right: God made the body of Adam out of the ground, and formed Eve from the body of Adam.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Genesis 2:7 says God breathed the breath of life into Adam and he became a living being. It does not mention a soul or say that it could never die; that is church teaching on the soul's immortality.
creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.doubt: The shown verses do not support "could never die." Genesis 3:19 speaks of returning to dust, and Genesis 3:22 implies Adam could have lived forever only by eating from the tree of life, which suggests he was not created with unending life.

before.question: What did God give Adam and Eve besides bodies?
before.answer: He gave them souls that could never die.
before.right: He gave them souls that could never die.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Matthew 10:28 distinguishes soul from body and says men cannot kill the soul, so the soul outlives the body's death. It does not say the soul can never die.
creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.doubt: Matthew 10:28 says God can destroy both soul and body in hell, and Ezekiel 18:4 says the soul who sins will die, so "can never die" goes beyond these verses.

before.question: Have you a soul as well as a body?
before.answer: Yes; I have a soul that can never die.
before.right: Yes; I have a soul that can never die.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Colossians 1:16 says all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, and Genesis 1:1 says God created the heavens and the earth. Together they teach that God made all things.

before.question: What else did God make?

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: No shown verse says that thinking about God and the world to come proves a soul. 1 Corinthians 2:11 only says a man's thoughts are known to the spirit within him, which is close but not the stated argument.

before.question: How do you know that you have a soul?
before.answer: Because I can think about God and the world to come.
before.right: Because I can think about God and the world to come.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: God saw all He had made and called it very good (1:31), and blessed Adam and Eve and gave them dominion (1:28). Holiness and happiness are drawn from this, not stated in these words.
creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.doubt: The shown text says "very good" and records God's blessing, but never uses the word "holy"; the answer's "holy" goes beyond these verses.

before.question: In what condition did God make Adam and Eve?
before.answer: He made them holy and happy.
before.right: He made them holy and happy.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Laban proposes to Jacob, "let us make a covenant, you and I," and God makes a covenant with Israel including those not present, showing a covenant as an agreement between parties.

before.question: What is a covenant?
before.answer: An agreement between two or more persons.
before.right: An agreement between two or more persons.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: God gives Adam a command with a condition: eat freely, but eating from the tree brings death. Hosea 6:7 says Israel, like Adam, transgressed the covenant, so the arrangement is called a covenant. "Covenant of works" is a theological label drawn from these verses.

before.question: What covenant did God make with Adam?

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: God commands Adam to eat freely of the garden but not from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, on pain of death. Adam is bound to keep that command; Hosea 6:7 says he transgressed the covenant.

before.question: What was Adam bound to do by the covenant of works?

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: God commands Adam to eat freely of the garden but not from the tree of knowledge, warning that he will surely die. The promise of life for obedience is implied by that warning, not stated outright.

before.question: What did God promise in the covenant of works?
before.answer: To reward Adam with life if he obeyed him.
before.right: To reward Adam with life if he obeyed him.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: God told Adam that eating from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil would bring death: "in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die."

before.question: What did God threaten in the covenant of works?
before.answer: To punish Adam with death if he disobeyed.
before.right: To punish Adam with death if he disobeyed.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Adam ate the forbidden fruit (Gen 3:6), and God says he ate from the tree He had commanded him not to eat (Gen 3:17), so Adam disobeyed God rather than keeping the covenant.

before.question: Did Adam keep the covenant of works?

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Psalm 78:10 describes people who failed to keep God's covenant and refused His law (doing), and Acts 8:21 says a heart "not right before God" (being). Together they teach the answer.

before.question: What is meant by want of conformity?
before.answer: Not being or doing what God requires.
before.right: Not being or doing what God requires.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Isaiah 43:7 says God's people were "created for My glory," which states the answer directly. Revelation 4:11 supports it by ascribing glory to God as Creator of all things.

before.question: Why did God make you and all things?

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Transgression is breaking God's covenant by doing what He forbids: Israelites who worship other gods are transgressing His covenant, "which I have forbidden." Daniel 9:11 likewise says Israel "transgressed Your law."

before.question: What is meant by transgression?

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Romans 5:18-19 says one man's trespass brought condemnation for all, and his disobedience made the many sinners, so Adam's act bound all his posterity. The words "covenant of works" are not in the verses.

before.question: Did Adam act for himself alone in the covenant of works?
before.answer: No; he represented all his posterity.
before.right: No; he represented all his posterity.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Romans 5:12 says death passed on to all men because all sinned, and Romans 5:19 says through one man's disobedience the many were made sinners. Together they teach the sin and misery in the answer, though "born" is an inference.

before.question: What effect had the sin of Adam on all mankind?
before.answer: All mankind are born in a state of sin and misery.
before.right: All mankind are born in a state of sin and misery.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Romans 5:12 says death passed to all because all sinned through Adam, and Psalm 51:5 says the psalmist was sinful from conception. The inherited sinful condition is taught there, though the term "original sin" itself does not appear.

before.question: What is that sinful nature which we inherit from Adam called?

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Jesus says no one can see or enter the kingdom of God unless born again of water and the Spirit, since flesh is born of flesh and spirit of the Spirit. The answer's need for a changed heart follows from this new birth.

before.question: Can any one go to heaven with this sinful nature?
before.answer: No, our hearts must be changed before we can be fit for heaven.
before.right: No, our hearts must be changed before we can be fit for heaven.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Jesus says no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again, and John 3:5-7 adds birth of water and the Spirit. The word "regeneration" itself does not appear, but the new birth it names is taught there.

before.question: What is a change of heart called?

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: 1 Corinthians 10:31 calls us to do everything for God's glory, and 1 John 5:3 says the love of God is keeping His commandments. Together they teach the answer.

before.question: How can you glorify God?
before.answer: By loving him and doing what he commands.
before.right: By loving him and doing what he commands.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Jesus says no one enters God's kingdom unless born of the Spirit; flesh gives birth only to flesh, and the new birth is by the Spirit, as the wind moves where it wishes.

before.question: Who can change a sinner's heart?

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Galatians 3:10-11 says those who rely on works of the law are under a curse and that no one is justified before God by the law, so the law-works route saves no one.

before.question: Can any one be saved through the covenant of works?
before.answer: None can be saved through the covenant of works.
before.right: None can be saved through the covenant of works.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Romans 3:23 says all have sinned, so all have broken the law. Galatians 3:10 says everyone who relies on works of the law is under a curse, which is the condemnation the answer describes.

before.question: Why can none be saved through the covenant of works?
before.answer: Because all have broken it, and are condemned by it.
before.right: Because all have broken it, and are condemned by it.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: 2 Timothy 1:9 says grace was given us in Christ Jesus before time began, which points to a pre-temporal arrangement centered on the Son. The verse never uses the word covenant or names the parties.

before.question: With whom did God the Father make the covenant of grace?

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Hebrews 9:15 calls Christ the mediator of the new covenant so that "those who are called" receive the eternal inheritance, and He died to redeem them. The verse says "called," not "elect," so "elect" is the catechism's doctrinal term for those people.

before.question: Whom did Christ represent in the covenant of grace?

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Galatians 4:4-5 says Christ was born under the law to redeem those under the law, and Hebrews 9:15 says he died to redeem them from their transgressions. Together these teach both parts of the answer.

before.question: What did Christ undertake in the covenant of grace?
before.answer: To keep the whole law for his people, and to suffer the punishment due to their sins.
before.right: To keep the law for his people and suffer the penalty for sins

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Hebrews 7:26 calls Christ holy, innocent and undefiled, and 1 Peter 2:22 says plainly, "He committed no sin," so the answer comes from these verses.

before.question: Did our Lord Jesus Christ ever commit the least sin?
before.answer: No; he was holy, innocent and undefiled.
before.right: No; he was holy, innocent and undefiled.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Hebrews 2:14 says the Son "shared in their humanity" (flesh and blood), Hebrews 2:18 says He "suffered when He was tempted," and Hebrews 5:8 says He learned obedience from what He suffered.

before.question: How could the Son of God suffer?
before.answer: Christ, the Son of God, became man that he might obey and suffer in our nature.
before.right: Christ became man to obey and suffer in our nature

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Romans 3:25-26 presents Christ's blood as the atoning sacrifice, showing God's justice while justifying believers. 2 Cor 5:21 says God made Him sin on our behalf, supporting the substitution in the answer.

before.question: What is meant by the Atonement?
before.answer: Christ's satisfying divine justice, by his sufferings and death, in the place of sinners.
before.right: Christ's satisfying divine justice by his sufferings and death for sinners

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Romans 8:29-30 shows God's foreknowing, predestining, calling, and justifying of His people. 1 Peter 1:2 adds God the Father's foreknowledge and the Spirit's sanctifying. Hebrews 9:15 ties the called to Christ's death that redeems them.
creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.doubt: Romans 8:29-30 names justification but not sanctification, and it does not mention Christ's death; those parts rest on 1 Peter 1:2 and Hebrews 9:15 and on the wider covenant framing.

before.question: What did God the Father undertake in the covenant of grace?
before.answer: To justify and sanctify those for whom Christ should die.
before.right: To justify and sanctify those for whom Christ should die.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Psalm 100:3 says the LORD made us and we are His people and the sheep of His pasture. "Made" is stated; the shepherd image teaches that He cares for us.

before.question: Why ought you to glorify God?
before.answer: Because he made me and takes care of me.
before.right: Because he made me and takes care of me.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Paul prays that God Himself will sanctify believers completely, keeping their whole spirit, soul, and body blameless. The answer's wording about heart and conduct is drawn from this and related verses.

before.question: What is sanctification?
before.answer: It is God's making sinners holy in heart and conduct.
before.right: It is God's making sinners holy in heart and conduct.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: John 17:2 says the Father gave a people to the Son, and the Son gives eternal life to all whom the Father has given Him. The answer follows from that, though the verse does not mention obedience or suffering.

before.question: For whom did Christ obey and suffer?
before.answer: For those whom the Father had given him.
before.right: For those whom the Father had given him.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Luke 9:58 shows Christ's poverty: He has no place to lay His head. Isaiah 53:3 shows His suffering: a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief, despised and rejected.

before.question: What kind of life did Christ live on earth?
before.answer: A life of poverty and suffering.
before.right: A life of poverty and suffering.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Philippians 2:8 says Christ became obedient to death, even death on a cross. Hebrews 12:2 says He endured the cross, scorning its shame. "Painful" is implied by enduring the cross rather than stated outright.

before.question: What kind of death did Christ die?
before.answer: The painful and shameful death of the cross.
before.right: The painful and shameful death of the cross.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Paul preaches repentance to God and faith in the Lord Jesus (Acts 20:21), and Hebrews 12:14 says holiness is necessary, without which no one will see the Lord.
creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.doubt: Heb 12:14 speaks of seeing the Lord rather than of being saved, and "only" is the catechism's own emphasis, though the verses do require all three.

before.question: Who will be saved?
before.answer: Only those who repent of sin, believe in Christ and lead holy lives.
before.right: Only those who repent, believe in Christ, and lead holy lives

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Sorrow for sin appears in 2 Corinthians 7:10 ("Godly sorrow brings repentance"), and forsaking one's way in Isaiah 55:7. Hating sin and its displeasing to God are not stated in these verses.

before.question: What is it to repent?
before.answer: To be sorry for sin, and to hate and forsake it because it is displeasing to God.
before.right: To be sorry for sin, and to hate and forsake it because it is displeasing to God.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Acts 16:31 says to believe in the Lord Jesus for salvation, and Ephesians 2:8-9 says we are saved through faith, not by works. Trusting Christ alone follows from these verses.

before.question: What is it to believe or have faith in Christ?
before.answer: To trust in Christ alone for salvation.
before.right: To trust in Christ alone for salvation.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: John 6:44 says no one can come to Christ unless the Father draws him; Philippians 2:13 says God works in us both to will and to act. Together they teach that we cannot believe or turn by our own power.

before.question: Can you repent and believe in Christ by your own power?
before.answer: No; I can do nothing good without the help of God's Holy Spirit.
before.right: No; I can do nothing good without God's Holy Spirit

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Jesus says the Father will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him, so the Spirit is received by asking God in prayer.

before.question: How can you get the help of the Holy Spirit?
before.answer: God has told us that we must pray to him for the Holy Spirit.
before.right: God has told us we must pray for the Holy Spirit

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: No shown verse gives a span of years since Christ's death. The figure comes from historical dating of the crucifixion, which places it roughly two thousand years before the present.

before.question: About how long ago did Christ die?

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Abraham believed God and it was credited as righteousness, and the people of Hebrews 11 died in faith, welcoming the promises from afar. Scripture teaches faith in God's promises before Christ, though the shown verses do not name a Saviour.

before.question: How were pious persons saved before the coming of Christ?
before.answer: By believing in a Saviour to come.
before.right: By believing in a Saviour to come.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Hebrews 11:4 says Abel offered God a sacrifice by faith, and Hebrews 10:1 calls the law's sacrifices a shadow of good things to come. The altar is not mentioned.

before.question: How did pious persons before Christ show their faith in the Saviour to come?
before.answer: By offering sacrifices on God's altar.
before.right: By offering sacrifices on God's altar.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Hebrews 10:1 calls the law's sacrifices a shadow of the good things to come, and John 1:29 names Jesus the Lamb of God who takes away sin.

before.question: What did these sacrifices represent?
before.answer: Christ, the Lamb of God, who was to die for sinners.
before.right: Christ, the Lamb of God, who was to die for sinners.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: None of the shown verses names Christ's three offices as prophet, priest, and king. The classification is church teaching drawn from scripture passages that treat Christ's work under each role, rather than from a single verse.

before.question: What are they?
before.answer: The offices of a prophet, of a priest, and of a king.
before.right: The offices of a prophet, of a priest, and of a king.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Hebrews 7:25 says Christ always lives to intercede for those who come to God, which is the pleading. Hebrews 7:27 says He sacrificed for sin once for all when He offered up Himself, which is the dying for our sins.

before.question: How is Christ a priest?
before.answer: Because he died for our sins and pleads with God for us.
before.right: Because he died for our sins and pleads with God for us.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Revelation 1:5 calls Jesus Christ the ruler of the kings of the earth. Psalm 89:18 calls the king "our shield" and "our king," which covers defense and rule. The psalm names the LORD, so applying it to Christ is a taught inference.

before.question: How is Christ a king?
before.answer: Because he rules over us and defends us.
before.right: Because he rules over us and defends us.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Jesus calls his disciples foolish and slow of heart to believe, then teaches them from the prophets, so the verse shows the need for Christ's teaching where people lack understanding.

before.question: Why do you need Christ as a prophet?

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: At Jesus's baptism the Son is baptized, the Spirit descends, and the Father speaks; 2 Corinthians 13:14 names the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the Holy Spirit together. The count of three persons follows from these.

before.question: In how many persons does this one God exist?

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Hebrews 2:17 says Christ became a high priest to make atonement for the sins of the people, so the need for a priest rests on sin and guilt.

before.question: Why do you need Christ as a priest?

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Romans 5:6 says that while we were still powerless, Christ died for the ungodly, which teaches our helplessness and our need for Christ. It does not speak of Christ as king.

before.question: Why do you need Christ as a king?
before.answer: Because I am weak and helpless.
before.right: Because I am weak and helpless.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Deuteronomy 4:13 calls the commandments God gave "the Ten Commandments," and Exodus 20:1-17 records them as the words God spoke at the mountain.

before.question: How many commandments did God give on Mount Sinai?

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Deuteronomy 4:13 calls them "the Ten Commandments," but the word "Decalogue" does not appear. It comes from the Greek for "ten words" (deka logoi), a later term for the same commandments.

before.question: What are the ten commandments sometimes called?

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: The first four commandments (Exod 20:3-11) concern worship of the LORD alone: no other gods, no idols, not taking His name in vain, and keeping the Sabbath holy. They teach duty to God.

before.question: What do the first four commandments teach?

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Exodus 20:12-17 gives the last six commandments: honor parents, do not murder, commit adultery, steal, bear false witness, or covet. Each concerns one's neighbor, so the answer follows from them.

before.question: What do the last six commandments teach?

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Psalm 147:11 says the LORD is pleased with those who fear Him and hope in His loving devotion; Proverbs 8:17 gives the quoted words, "I love those who love me."

before.question: Is God pleased with those who love and obey him?
before.answer: Yes; he says, 'I love those who love me.'
before.right: Yes; he says, 'I love those who love me.'

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Psalm 7:11 says God is a righteous judge who feels indignation each day, which the answer draws on. The verse does not name disobedience, but Psalm 7:12 and Hosea 9:17 tie God's displeasure to those who refuse to repent or obey.

before.question: Is God displeased with those who do not love and obey him?
before.answer: Yes; God is a righteous judge and a God who feels indignation each day.
before.right: Yes; God is a righteous judge and a God who feels indignation each day.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Matthew 28:19 names the three persons outright: baptizing "in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit." Matthew 3:16-17 shows all three present at Jesus' baptism.

before.question: What are they?
before.answer: The Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.
before.right: The Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Exodus 20:3 says "You shall have no other gods before Me." Forbidding other gods teaches that God alone is to be worshiped, which the catechism answer states plainly.

before.question: What does the first commandment teach us?

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Exodus 20:7 forbids taking God's name in vain. Psalm 138:2 exalts God's name and word, and Psalm 78:7 speaks of not forgetting His works, so together they teach reverence for name, word, and works.

before.question: What does the third commandment teach us?
before.answer: To reverence God's name, word, and works.
before.right: To reverence God's name, word, and works.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Acts 20:7 says the believers met "on the first day of the week," and Revelation 1:10 calls that day "the Lord's day." Neither verse uses the word Sabbath.

before.question: What day of the week is the Christian Sabbath?
before.answer: The first day of the week, called the Lord's day.
before.right: The first day of the week, called the Lord's day.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Matthew 28:1 and 28:6 show the resurrection occurred on the first day of the week, but no shown verse says why that day is called the Lord's day. The naming comes from church tradition.

before.question: Why is it called the Lord's day?
before.answer: Because on that day Christ rose from the dead.
before.right: Because on that day Christ rose from the dead.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: John 4:24 says plainly that "God is Spirit." The denial of a body like men is not stated there but follows from calling God Spirit.

before.question: What is God?
before.answer: God is a Spirit, and has not a body like men.
before.right: God is a Spirit, and has not a body like men.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Jesus enters the synagogue on the Sabbath to read Scripture (Luke 4:16), it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath (Matthew 12:12), and praising the LORD is good (Psalm 92:1). The verses shown do not name prayer.

before.question: How should the Sabbath be spent?
before.answer: In prayer and praise, in hearing and reading God's word, and in doing good to our fellow-men.
before.right: In prayer, praise, hearing God's word, and doing good to others

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:catechis.note: Exodus 20:13 forbids murder, and Colossians 3:8 commands believers to put aside anger and rage. Together they teach avoiding angry passions, though the link to the sixth commandment is drawn by inference.

before.question: What does the sixth commandment teach us?

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: The answer is a summary drawn from its proof texts: we are not our own but the Lord's, bought with precious blood, kept by the Father's will (Matt 10:29-30), and all things work together for good (Rom 8:28).

before.question: What is your only comfort in life and death?
before.answer: That I am not my own, but belong with body and soul, both in life and in death, to my faithful Saviour Jesus Christ. He has fully paid for all my sins with His precious blood, and has set me free from all the power of the devil. He also preserves me in such a way that without the will of my heavenly Father not a hair can fall from my head; indeed, all things must work together for my salvation. Therefore, by His Holy Spirit He also assures me of eternal life and makes me heartily willing and ready from now on to live for Him.
before.right: I belong to Jesus Christ who paid for all my sins and ensures all things work for my salvation

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Exodus 34:7 says God "will by no means leave the guilty unpunished," and Galatians 3:10 quotes the exact "Cursed is everyone who does not continue..." line. The "now and eternally" and original-sin points are supported elsewhere (Rom 1:18, Rom 5:12, Heb 9:27).

before.question: Will God allow such disobedience and apostasy to go unpunished?
before.answer: Certainly not. He is terribly displeased with our original sin as well as our actual sins. Therefore He will punish them by a just judgment both now and eternally, as He has declared: "Cursed is everyone who does not continue to do everything written in the Book of the Law."
before.right: Certainly not. God will punish both original and actual sins by just judgment now and eternally

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Leviticus 24:16 states that whoever blasphemes the LORD's name must be put to death, which supports the answer's claim that God commanded blasphemers to be punished with death. The claim that no sin is greater or provokes more wrath is not stated in the shown verses.
creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.doubt: The superlative "no sin is greater or provokes God's wrath more" is not stated in the shown verses; Leviticus 24:16 shows only the death penalty, and Leviticus 5:1 does not speak of blasphemy.

before.question: Is the blaspheming of God's Name by swearing and cursing such a grievous sin that God is angry also with those who do not prevent and forbid it as much as they can?
before.answer: Certainly, for no sin is greater or provokes God's wrath more than the blaspheming of His Name. That is why He commanded it to be punished with death.
before.right: Certainly. No sin provokes God's wrath more than blaspheming His Name, which He commanded to be punished with death.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Deut 6:13 commands Israel to take oaths in the LORD's name, and Heb 6:16 says oaths confirm and end argument. Saints such as Paul (2 Cor 1:23) swore this way. The government and necessity limits are the answer's own application, not stated in these verses.

before.question: But may we swear an oath by the Name of God in a godly manner?
before.answer: Yes, when the government demands it of its subjects, or when necessity requires it, in order to maintain and promote fidelity and truth, to God's glory and for our neighbour's good. Such oath-taking is based on God's Word and was therefore rightly used by saints in the Old and the New Testament.
before.right: Yes, when government demands or necessity requires, to maintain truth and fidelity for God's glory and neighbour's good.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Christ forbids swearing by heaven, earth, or other creatures (Matt 5:34-37; James 5:12). Swearing by heaven or the temple is really swearing by God who dwells there (Matt 23:21-22). Paul calls God as witness (2 Cor 1:23).

before.question: May we also swear by saints or other creatures?
before.answer: No. A lawful oath is a calling upon God, who alone knows the heart, to bear witness to the truth, and to punish me if I swear falsely. No creature is worthy of such honour.
before.right: No. Lawful oath calls upon God alone, who knows our heart, to witness truth. No creature deserves such honour.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Children are told to obey parents and to honor them, and everyone is to submit to governing authorities appointed by God. The answer's patience with parents' weaknesses is not stated in these verses.

before.question: What does God require in the fifth commandment?
before.answer: That I show all honour, love, and faithfulness to my father and mother and to all those in authority over me, submit myself with due obedience to their good instruction and discipline, and also have patience with their weaknesses and shortcomings, since it is God's will to govern us by their hand.
before.right: Show honour, love, and faithfulness to parents and authorities; obey their instruction; bear their weaknesses; God governs by them.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Matthew 5:21-22 forbids anger, insulting words, and murder; Leviticus 19:17-18 forbids hatred and revenge; Romans 13:4 gives the government the sword; Matthew 4:7 is the only shown verse near self-harm, and it speaks of testing God.

before.question: What does God require in the sixth commandment?
before.answer: I am not to dishonour, hate, injure, or kill my neighbour by thoughts, words, or gestures, and much less by deeds, whether personally or through another; rather, I am to put away all desire of revenge. Moreover, I am not to harm or recklessly endanger myself. Therefore, also, the government bears the sword to prevent murder.
before.right: Not to dishonour, hate, or kill by thought, word, or deed; put away revenge; not harm myself; government prevents murder.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: 1 John 3:15 says whoever hates his brother is a murderer, and Matthew 5:22 treats anger and insulting words as liable to judgment. Together they teach that God counts the root sins of hatred and anger as murder.

before.question: But does this commandment speak only of killing?
before.answer: By forbidding murder God teaches us that He hates the root of murder, such as envy, hatred, anger, and desire of revenge, and that He regards all these as murder.
before.right: God forbids the root of murder: envy, hatred, anger, and revenge, which He regards as murder.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Scripture commands loving the neighbour as oneself (Matt 22:39), clothing oneself with compassion, gentleness and patience (Col 3:12), and returning an enemy's stray ox or helping his fallen donkey (Exod 23:4-5).

before.question: Is it enough, then, that we do not kill our neighbour in any such way?
before.answer: No. God commands us to love our neighbour as ourselves, showing patience, gentleness, mercy, and doing good even to our enemies.
before.right: No. God commands us to love our neighbour as ourselves, showing patience, gentleness, mercy, and doing good even to our enemies.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Matthew 5:28 forbids lustful looking in the heart, 1 Corinthians 6:19 calls the body a temple of the Holy Spirit, and Ephesians 5:3-4 forbids even a hint of impurity, obscenity, or crude joking.

before.question: Does God in this commandment forbid nothing more than adultery and similar shameful sins?
before.answer: Since we, body and soul, are temples of the Holy Spirit, it is God's will that we keep ourselves pure and holy. Therefore He forbids all unchaste acts, gestures, words, thoughts, desires, and whatever may entice us to unchastity.
before.right: Since we are temples of the Holy Spirit, God forbids all unchaste acts, words, thoughts, desires, and whatever entices us to unchastity.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Scripture pairs God's mercy with justice: He forgives iniquity yet will by no means leave the guilty unpunished (Exod 34:7). Jesus names eternal punishment, with soul and body destroyed in hell (Matt 25:46; Matt 10:28).

before.question: But is God not also merciful?
before.answer: God is indeed merciful, but He is also just. His justice requires that sin committed against the most high majesty of God also be punished with the most severe, that is, with everlasting, punishment of body and soul.
before.right: God is merciful but also just. Sin against His majesty requires everlasting punishment of body and soul

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Matthew 7:12 gives the rule to do to others as you would have them do to you; Ephesians 4:28 says to work and do good so you may share with the needy; Galatians 6:10 says to do good to everyone as opportunity allows.

before.question: What does God require of you in this commandment?
before.answer: I must promote my neighbour's good wherever I can and may, deal with him as I would like others to deal with me, and work faithfully so that I may be able to give to those in need.
before.right: Promote my neighbour's good, treat him as I wish to be treated, work faithfully to give to those in need.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: The law's command "Do not covet" exposes desire as sin (Rom 7:7), David hates sin with perfect hatred (Ps 139:22), and God's precepts bring joy to the heart (Ps 19:8).

before.question: What does the tenth commandment require of us?
before.answer: That not even the slightest thought or desire contrary to any of God's commandments should ever arise in our heart. Rather, we should always hate all sin with all our heart, and delight in all righteousness.
before.right: No thought or desire against any commandment should arise; hate all sin with all heart and delight in all righteousness.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: No one is without sin, and Paul struggles with unfulfilled desire, yet he delights in God's law and presses on toward perfection, so the answer follows from these verses.

before.question: But can those converted to God keep these commandments perfectly?
before.answer: No. In this life even the holiest have only a small beginning of this obedience. Nevertheless, with earnest purpose they do begin to live not only according to some but to all the commandments of God.
before.right: No. The holiest have only a small beginning of this obedience, yet earnestly begin to live according to all God's commandments.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Romans 3:20 says the law brings awareness of sin, and Romans 3:24 says we are justified by grace in Christ. Philippians 3:12-14 describes pressing on toward the goal of perfection, not yet attained.

before.question: If in this life no one can keep the ten commandments perfectly, why does God have them preached so strictly?
before.answer: First, that throughout our life we may more and more become aware of our sinful nature, and therefore seek more eagerly the forgiveness of sins and righteousness in Christ. Second, that we may be zealous for good deeds and constantly pray to God for the grace of the Holy Spirit, that He may more and more renew us after God's image, until after this life we reach the goal of perfection.
before.right: So we see our sin and seek Christ, pursue good deeds and prayer, and grow more in God's image.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Psalm 50:14-15 pairs thanksgiving with calling on God in the day of trouble, and Luke 11:13 says the Father gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask. "Most important part" is the catechism's emphasis, not a stated ranking.

before.question: Why is prayer necessary for Christians?
before.answer: Because prayer is the most important part of the thankfulness which God requires of us. Moreover, God will give His grace and the Holy Spirit only to those who constantly and with heartfelt longing ask Him for these gifts and thank Him for them.
before.right: Prayer is necessary because it's most important to the thankfulness God requires; He gives grace and Holy Spirit only to those asking constantly.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Prayer must call on the Lord in truth and spirit, Daniel humbly pleads not for his righteous acts but for God's compassion, and Jesus promises to answer prayer asked in His name.

before.question: What belongs to a prayer which pleases God and is heard by Him?
before.answer: First, we must from the heart call upon the one true God only, who has revealed Himself in His Word, for all that He has commanded us to pray. Second, we must thoroughly know our need and misery, so that we may humble ourselves before God. Third, we must rest on this firm foundation that, although we do not deserve it, God will certainly hear our prayer for the sake of Christ our Lord, as He has promised us in His Word.
before.right: Call upon God revealed in His Word; know our need to humble ourselves; trust God hears for Christ's sake.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Jesus says "this is how you should pray" and gives the Lord's Prayer. Its petitions cover bodily need (daily bread) and the soul (forgiveness, deliverance from evil), so the answer follows from it.

before.question: What has God commanded us to ask of Him?
before.answer: All the things we need for body and soul, as included in the prayer which Christ our Lord Himself taught us.
before.right: All the things we need for body and soul, as included in the prayer which Christ our Lord Himself taught us.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Jesus says, "this is how you should pray," then gives the prayer in Matthew 6:9-13, which matches the catechism's answer phrase by phrase.

before.question: What is the Lord's prayer?
before.answer: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be Your name. Your kingdom come, Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one.
before.right: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be Your name. Your kingdom come. Give us daily bread, forgive us, and deliver us from the evil one.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: God will not acquit the guilty (Exod 23:7) and repays each by his deeds (Rom 2:6), so the penalty must be paid by us or by another; the Servant bears iniquities (Isa 53:11) and God sends His Son as an offering for sin (Rom 8:3).

before.question: Since, according to God's righteous judgment we deserve temporal and eternal punishment, how can we escape this punishment and be again received into favour?
before.answer: God demands that His justice be satisfied. Therefore full payment must be made either by ourselves or by another.
before.right: God demands that His justice be satisfied. Full payment must be made by ourselves or another.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Matthew 7:9-11 teaches that the Father in heaven gives good things to those who ask Him, far more than earthly fathers give to their children. The "childlike reverence" purpose is the catechism's own inference, not stated in these verses.

before.question: Why has Christ commanded us to address God as Our Father?
before.answer: To awaken in us at the very beginning of our prayer that childlike reverence and trust toward God which should be basic to our prayer: God has become our Father through Christ and will much less deny us what we ask of Him in faith than our fathers would refuse us earthly things.
before.right: To awaken childlike reverence and trust; God through Christ became our Father and gives us what we ask in faith.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: God is not only a God nearby but fills heaven and earth, so His heavenly majesty is not earthly; and your heavenly Father knows your needs and will freely give all things, as Matthew 6:32-33 and Romans 8:32 say.

before.question: Why is there added, "in heaven" in the words "Our Father in heaven"?
before.answer: These words teach us not to think of God's heavenly majesty in an earthly manner, and to expect from His almighty power all things we need for body and soul.
before.right: Not to think of God's majesty in an earthly manner, and to expect all things we need from His almighty power.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Matthew 6:9 gives the prayer as "Our Father in heaven, hallowed be Your name," with that petition first, before "Your kingdom come" in verse 10.

before.question: What is the first petition of the Lord's Prayer?
before.answer: Hallowed be Your name. That is: Grant us first of all that we may rightly know You, and sanctify, glorify, and praise You in all Your works, in which shine forth Your almighty power, wisdom, goodness, righteousness, mercy, and truth. Grant us also that we may so direct our whole life—our thoughts, words, and actions—that Your name is not blasphemed because of us but always honored and praised.
before.right: That we rightly know God, praise Him in all His works, and live so His name is honored, not blasphemed.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Jesus teaches the prayer "Your kingdom come, Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven," which is the second petition; the catechism's added explanation draws on its listed proof texts.

before.question: What is the second petition?
before.answer: Your kingdom come. That is: So rule us by Your Word and Spirit that more and more we submit to You. Preserve and increase Your church. Destroy the works of the devil, every power that raises itself against You, and every conspiracy against Your holy Word. Do all this until the fullness of Your kingdom comes, in which You will be all in all.
before.right: God ruling us by His Word and Spirit, preserving His church, destroying the devil's works, until His kingdom comes.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Matthew 6:12 states the fifth petition: "And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors." The catechism's added explanation rests on the other shown passages, such as Romans 8:1 and 1 John 2:1-2.

before.question: What is the fifth petition?
before.answer: And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors. That is: For the sake of Christ's blood, do not impute to us, wretched sinners, any of our transgressions, nor the evil which still clings to us, as we also find this evidence of Your grace in us that we are fully determined wholeheartedly to forgive our neighbor.
before.right: For Christ's blood, do not impute our sins to us; evidence of God's grace is that we wholeheartedly forgive our neighbors.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Matthew 6:13 gives the petition itself: "And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one." The printed answer's explanation draws on the question's reference verses, such as Ephesians 6 and 1 Peter 5:8.

before.question: What is the sixth petition?
before.answer: And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one. That is: In ourselves we are so weak that we cannot stand even for a moment. Moreover, our sworn enemies-- the devil, the world, and our own flesh-- do not cease to attack us. Will You, therefore, uphold and strengthen us by the power of Your Holy Spirit, so that in this spiritual war we may not go down to defeat, but always firmly resist our enemies, until we finally obtain the complete victory.
before.right: Ask God to strengthen us by His Holy Spirit, since we are too weak to resist our enemies.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: The closing words are the doxology, which the BSB's Matthew 6:13 omits (it ends at "the evil one"); it is a later addition absent from the earliest manuscripts. Psalm 115:1 and Romans 10:12 support the explanation.
creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.doubt: The printed answer gives the doxology as the conclusion, but no shown verse contains those words; the BSB text of Matthew 6:13 ends before them.

before.question: How do you conclude your prayer?
before.answer: For yours is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, forever. That is: All this we ask of You because, as our King, having power over all things, You are both willing and able to give us all that is good, and because not we but Your holy name should receive all glory forever.
before.right: For yours is the kingdom, power, and glory forever. You are King over all, willing and able to grant our requests.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: No shown verse defines Amen as "true and certain"; that meaning comes from the Hebrew word's sense of firmness. The second sentence rests on Isaiah 65:24, where God hears before people call.

before.question: What does the word Amen mean?
before.answer: Amen means: It is true and certain. For God has much more certainly heard my prayer than I feel in my heart that I desire this of Him.
before.right: It is true and certain; God has more certainly heard my prayer than I feel my desire in my heart.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Psalm 130:3 implies no one could stand if God kept track of iniquities, so we cannot pay. Romans 2:5 says the unrepentant heart is storing up wrath, which matches our increasing debt.

before.question: Can we ourselves make this payment?
before.answer: Certainly not. On the contrary, we daily increase our debt.
before.right: Certainly not. On the contrary, we daily increase our debt.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Ezekiel 18:20 says a son will not bear his father's iniquity and the soul who sins will die, so God does not punish another for sin. Nahum 1:6 asks who can endure His burning anger, showing no creature can bear it.

before.question: Can any mere creature pay for us?
before.answer: No. In the first place, God will not punish another creature for the sin which man has committed. Furthermore, no mere creature can sustain the burden of God's eternal wrath against sin and deliver others from it.
before.right: No. God will not punish another creature for man's sin, nor can any creature sustain God's eternal wrath

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Isaiah 9:6 names the child born and son given as "Mighty God," and Hebrews 7:26 describes a high priest who is holy, innocent, and undefiled, so the answer's true man and true God follow from these verses.

before.question: What kind of mediator and deliverer must we seek?
before.answer: One who is a true and righteous man, and yet more powerful than all creatures; that is, one who is at the same time true God.
before.right: One who is a true and righteous man and also true God, more powerful than all creatures

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Hebrews 2:14-17 shows He shared flesh and blood and was made like His brothers to make atonement. Hebrews 7:26-27 shows He is holy, innocent, and undefiled, so He had no sins of His own to offer for. The "justice of God" wording is an inference from these.

before.question: Why must He be a true and righteous man?
before.answer: He must be a true man because the justice of God requires that the same human nature which has sinned should pay for sin. He must be a righteous man because one who himself is a sinner cannot pay for others.
before.right: He must be truly human so human nature can pay for sin, and righteous so He can pay for others

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: The Child is called "Mighty God" (Isa 9:6). No one can withstand God's wrath (Nah 1:6), yet the Servant is punished for our sins (Isa 53:5) and we become God's righteousness in Him (2 Cor 5:21).

before.question: Why must He at the same time be true God?
before.answer: He must be true God so that by the power of His divine nature He might bear in His human nature the burden of God's wrath, and might obtain for us and restore to us righteousness and life.
before.right: By His divine power He can bear God's wrath, obtaining and restoring for us righteousness and life

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: 1 Corinthians 1:30 names Christ Jesus as our wisdom, righteousness, holiness, and redemption; 1 Timothy 2:5 calls him the mediator, "the man Christ Jesus"; 1 John 5:20 says he is the true God.

before.question: But who is that Mediator who at the same time is true God and a true and righteous man?
before.answer: Our Lord Jesus Christ, who became to us wisdom from God—our righteousness, holiness, and redemption.
before.right: Our Lord Jesus Christ, who became to us wisdom from God, our righteousness, holiness, and redemption

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: The answer rests on the verses: God first promised the woman's seed in Paradise (Gen 3:15), spoke through the prophets and then through His Son (Heb 1:1-2), and the law's sacrifices were a shadow of the good things to come (Heb 10:1).

before.question: From where do you know this?
before.answer: From the holy gospel, which God Himself first revealed in Paradise. Later, He had it proclaimed by the patriarchs and prophets, and foreshadowed by the sacrifices and other ceremonies of the law. Finally, He had it fulfilled through His only Son.
before.right: From the gospel: God revealed it in Paradise, proclaimed by patriarchs and prophets, foreshadowed in the law

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: The three parts follow the catechism's proof texts: Romans 3:9-10 shows human sin, Acts 10:43 shows forgiveness through Jesus' name, and Romans 6:13 calls believers to present themselves to God in gratitude.

before.question: What do you need to know in order to live and die in the joy of this comfort?
before.answer: First, how great my sins and misery are; second, how I am delivered from all my sins and misery; third, how I am to be thankful to God for such deliverance.
before.right: How great my sins and misery are; how I am delivered from them; how to be thankful

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Only those who believe have eternal life, while those who reject the Son remain under God's wrath. Believers are grafted in and stand by faith, while unbelieving branches were broken off.

before.question: Are all men, then, saved by Christ just as they perished through Adam?
before.answer: No. Only those are saved who by a true faith are grafted into Christ and accept all His benefits.
before.right: No. Only those are saved who by a true faith are grafted into Christ and accept all His benefits.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Hebrews 11:1 defines faith as assurance and certainty, Romans 3:24 says we are justified freely by grace through Christ, and Romans 10:17 says faith comes by hearing the word of Christ.

before.question: According to the Heidelberg Catechism, what is true faith?
before.answer: True faith is a sure knowledge whereby I accept as true all that God has revealed to us in His Word. At the same time it is a firm confidence that not only to others, but also to me, God has granted forgiveness of sins, everlasting righteousness, and salvation, out of mere grace, only for the sake of Christ's merits. This faith the Holy Spirit works in my heart by the gospel.
before.right: Sure knowledge of God's Word and firm confidence that Christ's merits save me by grace

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: John 20:31 says the gospel record is written so you may believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life; Galatians 3:22 ties the promise to faith in Christ. The creed summary is church teaching.

before.question: What, then, must a Christian believe?
before.answer: All that is promised us in the Gospel, which the articles of our catholic and undoubted Christian faith teach us in a summary.
before.right: All promised in the Gospel, which the articles of Christian faith teach in summary

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: No shown verse divides the creed into three parts. This threefold arrangement (Father, Son, Holy Spirit) is the catechism's own teaching, though passages like 1 Peter 1:2 and 1 Corinthians 8:6 name the same persons.

before.question: How are these articles divided?
before.answer: Into three parts: the first is about God the Father and our creation; the second about God the Son and our redemption; the third about God the Holy Spirit and our sanctification.
before.right: Into three parts: God the Father and creation; God the Son and redemption; God the Holy Spirit and sanctification

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: No verse states the answer outright, but together these verses teach it: the LORD is one (Deut 6:4), the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ are each named as the one God (1 Cor 8:6), and the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit share one "name" (Matt 28:19).

before.question: Since there is only one God, why do you speak of three persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit?
before.answer: Because God has so revealed Himself in His Word that these three distinct persons are the one, true, eternal God.
before.right: Because God revealed in His Word that these three distinct persons are the one, true God

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Gen 1:1, Ps 104:27-30 and Eph 1:11 show God creating, sustaining and governing all things; Rom 8:15-16, Matt 6:30, Rom 8:28, Gen 18:14 and Matt 7:9-11 show His fatherly care, power and good purpose. "Out of nothing" is inferred, not stated.

before.question: What do you believe when you say: I believe in God the Father almighty, Creator of heaven and earth?
before.answer: That the eternal Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who out of nothing created heaven and earth and all that is in them, and who still upholds and governs them by His eternal counsel and providence, is, for the sake of Christ His Son, my God and my Father. In Him I trust so completely as to have no doubt that He will provide me with all things necessary for body and soul, and will also turn to my good whatever adversity He sends me in this life of sorrow. He is able to do so as almighty God, and willing also as a faithful Father.
before.right: The eternal Father of Christ, Creator of all, who upholds all, is my God and Father in whom I trust

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Scripture teaches that the Son upholds all things by His powerful word, that not a sparrow falls apart from the Father's will, that the lot's every decision is from the LORD, and that God gives rain and fruitful seasons.

before.question: What do you understand by the providence of God?
before.answer: God's providence is His almighty and ever present power, whereby, as with His hand, He still upholds heaven and earth and all creatures, and so governs them that leaf and blade, rain and drought, fruitful and barren years, food and drink, health and sickness, riches and poverty, indeed, all things, come not by chance but by His fatherly hand.
before.right: God's almighty power by which He upholds all things and governs all creatures by His fatherly hand

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Job 1:21-22 shows patience in loss, Deuteronomy 8:10 calls for thanks in plenty, Romans 8:38-39 says nothing can separate us from God's love, and Job 1:12 and Proverbs 21:1 show creatures under God's hand.

before.question: What does it benefit us to know that God has created all things and still upholds them by His providence?
before.answer: We can be patient in adversity, thankful in prosperity, and with a view to the future we can have a firm confidence in our faithful God and Father that no creature shall separate us from His love; for all creatures are so completely in His hand that without His will they cannot so much as move.
before.right: We can be patient in adversity, thankful in prosperity, and confident no creature shall separate us from His love.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Matthew 1:21 says the Son will save His people from their sins, and Acts 4:12 says salvation exists in no one else, covering both parts of the answer.

before.question: Why is the Son of God called Jesus, that is, Saviour?
before.answer: Because He saves us from all our sins, and because salvation is not to be sought or found in anyone else.
before.right: Because He saves us from all our sins, and salvation is found in Him alone

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Romans 3:20 says the law brings awareness of sin, so knowledge of sin comes from the law of God. Misery is not stated here but follows from the same passage's teaching.

before.question: From where do you know your sins and misery?

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Christ holds all God's fullness, and believers are made complete in Him, while those seeking justification elsewhere are severed from Christ, so seeking salvation outside Him denies Him as Saviour.

before.question: Do those believe in the only Saviour Jesus who seek their salvation and well-being from saints, in themselves, or anywhere else?
before.answer: No. Though they boast of Him in words, they in fact deny the only Saviour Jesus. For one of two things must be true: either Jesus is not a complete Saviour, or those who by true faith accept this Saviour must find in Him all that is necessary for their salvation.
before.right: No, they deny that Jesus is the complete Saviour in whom all necessary salvation must be found

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: God anoints Him with the Spirit and above His companions (Ps 45:7; Isa 61:1), and the verses show Him as prophet (Deut 18:15), priest forever (Ps 110:4), and eternal king (Luke 1:33).

before.question: Why is He called Christ, that is, Anointed?
before.answer: Because He has been ordained by God the Father, and anointed with the Holy Spirit, to be our chief Prophet and Teacher, who has fully revealed to us the secret counsel and will of God concerning our redemption; our only High Priest, who by the one sacrifice of His body has redeemed us, and who continually intercedes for us before the Father; and our eternal King, who governs us by His Word and Spirit, and who defends and preserves us in the redemption obtained for us.
before.right: As God's anointed, He is our Prophet revealing God's will, our Priest who redeemed us through sacrifice, and our eternal King

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Believers are members of Christ's body (1 Cor 12:27), share His anointing (1 John 2:27), are a royal priesthood (1 Pet 2:9), fight the devil (Eph 6:11), and reign with Him (2 Tim 2:12).

before.question: Why are you called a Christian?
before.answer: Because I am a member of Christ by faith and thus share in His anointing, so that I may as prophet confess His Name, as priest present myself a living sacrifice of thankfulness to Him, and as king fight with a free and good conscience against sin and the devil in this life, and hereafter reign with Him eternally over all creatures.
before.right: Because I am a member of Christ by faith and share His anointing as prophet, priest, and king

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Christ is the one and only Son who is God and was with God in the beginning, while believers are predestined for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ, by grace in the Beloved.

before.question: Why is He called God's only begotten Son, since we also are children of God?
before.answer: Because Christ alone is the eternal, natural Son of God. We, however, are children of God by adoption, through grace, for Christ's sake.
before.right: Because Christ alone is God's eternal natural Son, while we are children of God by adoption through grace

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Peter says we were redeemed with the precious blood of Christ, not silver or gold; Hebrews says He freed us from the devil's power; Paul says we were bought at a price, so we are not our own.
