before.question: Why do you call Him our Lord?
before.answer: Because He has ransomed us, body and soul, from all our sins, not with silver or gold but with His precious blood, and has freed us from all the power of the devil to make us His own possession.
before.right: Because He ransomed us, body and soul, from sin and the devil's power with His precious blood

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: The Word who was God (John 1:1) became flesh (John 1:14) through the Holy Spirit's coming upon Mary (Luke 1:35), a descendant of David (Romans 1:3), made like His brothers yet without sin (Hebrews 2:17; 4:15).

before.question: What do you confess when you say: He was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the virgin Mary?
before.answer: The eternal Son of God, who is and remains true and eternal God, took upon Himself true human nature from the flesh and blood of the virgin Mary, through the working of the Holy Spirit. Thus He is also the true seed of David, and like His brothers in every respect, yet without sin.
before.right: The eternal Son of God took on true human nature from the virgin Mary through the Holy Spirit, remaining true God, without sin

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Christ is the one mediator between God and men (1 Tim 2:5). The sinless One was made sin for us so we might become God's righteousness (2 Cor 5:21). Psalm 51:5 shows the sin we were conceived in.

before.question: What benefit do you receive from the holy conception and birth of Christ?
before.answer: He is our Mediator, and with His innocence and perfect holiness covers, in the sight of God, my sin, in which I was conceived and born.
before.right: He is our Mediator and with His innocence and perfect holiness covers my sin before God

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Isaiah 53:5 and 53:10 show the Servant bearing our punishment as a guilt offering; 1 Peter 2:24 says He bore our sins in His body; 2 Corinthians 5:21 gives righteousness; 1 John 2:2 gives atonement for the whole world.

before.question: What do you confess when you say that He suffered?
before.answer: During all the time He lived on earth, but especially at the end, Christ bore in body and soul the wrath of God against the sin of the whole human race. Thus, by His suffering, as the only atoning sacrifice, He has redeemed our body and soul from everlasting damnation, and obtained for us the grace of God, righteousness, and eternal life.
before.right: That Christ bore God's wrath against the sin of humanity, and through His suffering as atoning sacrifice redeemed us

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Pilate declares Jesus not guilty yet sentences Him to the crowd's demand (Luke 23:14, 24). Christ redeemed us from the law's curse by becoming a curse for us (Gal 3:13), which supplies the freeing from judgment.

before.question: Why did He suffer under Pontius Pilate as judge?
before.answer: Though innocent, Christ was condemned by an earthly judge, and so He freed us from the severe judgment of God that was to fall on us.
before.right: Though innocent, Christ was condemned by an earthly judge, freeing us from God's severe judgment

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Galatians 3:13 says Christ became a curse for us, and Deuteronomy 21:23 says anyone hung on a tree is under God's curse. Together they teach that the cursed death Christ bore was hanging on a tree.

before.question: Does it have a special meaning that Christ was crucified and did not die in a different way?
before.answer: Yes. Thereby I am assured that He took upon Himself the curse which lay on me, for a crucified one was cursed by God.
before.right: Yes. Thereby I am assured that He took upon Himself the curse which lay on me

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Jesus names the greatest commandment as loving the Lord with all heart, soul and mind, and the second as loving one's neighbor as oneself, and says all the Law and Prophets hang on these two.

before.question: What does God's law require of us?
before.answer: Christ teaches us this in a summary in Matthew 22: "Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind. This is the first and greatest commandment. And the second is like it: 'Love your neighbor as yourself.' All the Law and the Prophets hang on these two commandments."
before.right: Love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, and mind; love your neighbor as yourself

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Romans 3:25-26 shows God setting forth Christ's blood as the atoning sacrifice to demonstrate His righteousness and be just; Romans 8:3 says the law was powerless, so God sent His Son as an offering for sin.

before.question: Why was it necessary for Christ to humble Himself even unto death?
before.answer: Because of the justice and truth of God satisfaction for our sins could be made in no other way than by the death of the Son of God.
before.right: Because God's justice and truth required that satisfaction for our sins be made only through death of God's Son

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Scripture does not state the purpose of the burial, but the accounts show Jesus' body placed in a tomb after death, and Paul lists "that He was buried" between His death and resurrection, so the answer follows from them.

before.question: Why was he buried?
before.answer: His burial testified that He had really died.
before.right: His burial testified that He had really died.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Romans 6:7 says the one who has died is freed from sin, Philippians 1:23 speaks of departing to be with Christ, and 1 Thessalonians 5:10 says we will live with Him. Together they teach the answer's second half.
creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.doubt: The shown verses do not say outright that our death is not a payment for sins; Romans 6:23 calls death the wages of sin, so that clause rests on the wider teaching that Christ alone paid.

before.question: Since Christ has died for us, why do we still have to die?
before.answer: Our death is not a payment for our sins, but it puts an end to sin and is an entrance into eternal life.
before.right: Our death is not payment for our sins but ends sin and enters eternal life

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Romans 6:4 says we were buried with Christ, and Romans 6:6 says our old self was crucified with Him so sin's body is powerless. Romans 6:12 forbids sin to reign, and Romans 12:1 calls us to offer our bodies as living sacrifices.

before.question: What further benefit do we receive from Christ's sacrifice and death on the cross?
before.answer: Through Christ's death our old nature is crucified, put to death, and buried with Him, so that the evil desires of the flesh may no longer reign in us, but that we may offer ourselves to Him as a sacrifice of thankfulness.
before.right: Through Christ's death our old nature is crucified with Him so we may offer ourselves as a sacrifice to Him

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Isaiah 53 says the punishment that brought us peace fell on the Servant and that He suffered anguish of soul; Matthew 27:46 records His cry of abandonment on the cross. The answer follows from these.

before.question: Why is there added: He descended into hell?
before.answer: In my greatest sorrows and temptations I may be assured and comforted that my Lord Jesus Christ, by His unspeakable anguish, pain, terror, and agony, which He endured throughout all His sufferings but especially on the cross, has delivered me from the anguish and torment of hell.
before.right: So that through His unspeakable suffering and agony, especially on the cross, Christ delivered us from hell's torment

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Romans 4:25 ties Christ's resurrection to our justification, Ephesians 2:5-6 says God made us alive and raised us up with Christ, and 1 Corinthians 6:14 promises that God will raise us by His power.

before.question: How does Christ's resurrection benefit us?
before.answer: First, by His resurrection He has overcome death, so that He could make us share in the righteousness which He had obtained for us by His death. Second, by His power we too are raised up to a new life. Third, Christ's resurrection is to us a sure pledge of our glorious resurrection.
before.right: By His resurrection Christ overcame death, shares righteousness with us, raises us to new life, and pledges our glorious resurrection

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Acts 1:9 says the disciples watched as Jesus was taken up. Acts 1:11 promises His return. Heb 9:24 and Rom 8:34 say He now appears for us before God. The judgment of the living and dead is not stated in these verses.

before.question: What do you confess when you say, He ascended into heaven?
before.answer: That Christ, before the eyes of His disciples, was taken up from the earth into heaven, and that He is there for our benefit until He comes again to judge the living and the dead.
before.right: That Christ was taken up into heaven before His disciples and is there for our benefit until He comes to judge

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Jesus says He will no longer be in the world, going to the Father, yet promises to be with His people always. Colossians 2:9 says the full Deity dwells in Him in bodily form.

before.question: Is Christ, then, not with us until the end of the world, as He has promised us?
before.answer: Christ is true man and true God. With respect to His human nature He is no longer on earth, but with respect to His divinity, majesty, grace, and Spirit He is never absent from us.
before.right: By His divinity, majesty, grace, and Spirit Christ is never absent from us; by His human nature He is no longer on earth.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Jeremiah 23:23-24 teaches that the LORD fills heaven and earth and is not only nearby. Colossians 2:9 says the fullness of Deity dwells in Christ in bodily form, which supports the union of divinity with the human nature.

before.question: But are the two natures in Christ not separated from each other if His human nature is not present wherever His divinity is?
before.answer: Not at all, for His divinity has no limits and is present everywhere. So it must follow that His divinity is indeed beyond the human nature which He has taken on and nevertheless is within this human nature and remains personally united with it.
before.right: His divinity has no limits, is present everywhere, and is personally united with His human nature.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Christ is our advocate before the Father (1 John 2:1), prepares a place for us and will receive us to Himself (John 14:2-3), and the Spirit is given as a pledge (2 Cor 5:5), so we seek things above (Col 3:1-2).

before.question: How does Christ's ascension into heaven benefit us?
before.answer: First, He is our Advocate in heaven before His Father. Second, we have our flesh in heaven as a sure pledge that He, our Head, will also take us, His members, up to Himself. Third, He sends us His Spirit as a counter-pledge, by whose power we seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God, and not the things that are on earth.
before.right: Our Advocate in heaven; our flesh there pledges He will take us; Spirit sent enables us to seek heavenly things.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: All have sinned and fall short (Rom 3:23); the flesh's mind is hostile to God and cannot submit to His law (Rom 8:7); by nature we were children of wrath, hating one another (Eph 2:3; Titus 3:3).

before.question: Can you keep all this perfectly?
before.answer: No, I am inclined by nature to hate God and my neighbour.
before.right: No, I am inclined by nature to hate God and my neighbour.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Christ is seated at God's right hand and God made Him head over everything for the church, His body. Sitting there shows Him as exalted Head of the Church and ruler of all.

before.question: Why is it added, And sits at the right hand of God?
before.answer: Christ ascended into heaven to manifest Himself there as Head of His Church, through whom the Father governs all things.
before.right: Christ ascended to manifest Himself as Head of His Church, through whom the Father governs all things.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Acts 2:33 says the exalted Christ poured out the promised Holy Spirit; Psalm 110:1-2 has the Lord making His enemies a footstool and ruling in the midst of them, which supports His power defending His people.

before.question: How does the glory of Christ, our Head, benefit us?
before.answer: First, by His Holy Spirit He pours out heavenly gifts upon us, His members. Second, by His power He defends and preserves us against all enemies.
before.right: By His Spirit He pours out heavenly gifts; by His power He defends us against all enemies.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Christ, revealed from heaven, repays affliction to those who afflict His people and gives relief to the oppressed; Matthew 25 shows Him separating the cursed from the righteous, who enter eternal life.

before.question: What comfort is it to you that Christ will come to judge the living and the dead?
before.answer: In all my sorrow and persecution I lift up my head and eagerly await as judge from heaven the very same person who before has submitted Himself to the judgment of God for my sake, and has removed all the curse from me. He will cast all His and my enemies into everlasting condemnation, but He will take me and all His chosen ones to Himself into heavenly joy and glory.
before.right: Christ, who bore God's judgment for me, will judge my enemies and bring me to glory.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Acts 5:3-4 equates lying to the Holy Spirit with lying to God, showing He is God. John 14:16-17 promises another Advocate to be with us forever, and Galatians 3:14 says we receive the Spirit by faith.

before.question: What do you believe concerning the Holy Spirit?
before.answer: First, He is, together with the Father and the Son, true and eternal God. Second, He is also given to me, to make me by true faith share in Christ and all His benefits, to comfort me, and to remain with me forever.
before.right: He is true eternal God with Father and Son; given to share Christ with me, comfort me, and remain forever.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Christ says He will build His church against which the gates of Hades will not prevail, and no one can snatch His sheep from His hand. Revelation 5:9 says He purchased people from every nation, and Ephesians 1:4-5 says He chose us. Ephesians 4:13 and 5:26 add unity of faith and cleansing by the word.

before.question: What do you believe concerning the holy catholic Christian church?
before.answer: I believe that the Son of God, out of the whole human race, from the beginning of the world to its end, gathers, defends, and preserves for Himself, by His Spirit and Word, in the unity of the true faith, a church chosen to everlasting life. And I believe that I am and forever shall remain a living member of it.
before.right: Christ gathers the church from all time through His Spirit and Word in true faith, and I'm a living member.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Believers are members of one body in Christ and share fellowship with the Father and Son (1 Cor 12:12-13; 1 John 1:3), and each should use his gift to serve one another (1 Pet 4:10).

before.question: What do you understand by the communion of saints?
before.answer: First, that believers, all and everyone, as members of Christ have communion with Him and share in all His treasures and gifts. Second, that everyone is duty-bound to use his gifts readily and cheerfully for the benefit and well-being of the other members.
before.right: Believers as Christ's members share in His treasures and gifts; everyone must use their gifts for others' benefit.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: God says He will remember sins no more (Heb 10:17), makes us the righteousness of God in Christ (2 Cor 5:21), and there is now no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus (Rom 8:1). The sinful nature is not named as forgiven, so that part is drawn from the proof texts.

before.question: What do you believe concerning the forgiveness of sins?
before.answer: I believe that God, because of Christ's satisfaction, will no more remember my sins, nor my sinful nature, against which I have to struggle all my life, but He will graciously grant me the righteousness of Christ, that I may never come into condemnation.
before.right: God won't remember my sins or sinful nature against me but grants me Christ's righteousness so I never face condemnation.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Luke 23:43 says the believer goes to be with Christ that same day, and Philippians 3:21 says Christ will transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body. The reunion of flesh and soul is drawn from these.

before.question: What comfort does the resurrection of the body offer you?
before.answer: Not only shall my soul after this life immediately be taken up to Christ, my Head, but also this my flesh, raised by the power of Christ, shall be reunited with my soul and made like Christ's glorious body.
before.right: Soul goes to Christ; flesh is raised by His power, reunited with soul, made like His glorious body.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: 1 Corinthians 2:9 gives the unseen, unheard, unimagined blessing God has prepared, Romans 14:17 names present joy in the Holy Spirit, and John 17:24 promises believers will be with Christ to see His glory.

before.question: What comfort do you receive from the article about the life everlasting?
before.answer: Since I now already feel in my heart the beginning of eternal joy, I shall after this life possess perfect blessedness, such as no eye has seen, no ear has heard, no heart has imagined—a blessedness in which to praise God forever.
before.right: I already feel eternal joy's beginning in my heart; I will possess perfect blessedness beyond perception and praise God forever.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Romans 5:1 says believers are justified through faith and have peace with God through Christ; John 3:36 says whoever believes in the Son has eternal life. "Heir" is implied, not stated.

before.question: But what does it help you now that you believe all this?
before.answer: In Christ I am righteous before God and heir to life everlasting.
before.right: In Christ I am righteous before God and heir to life everlasting.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Genesis 1:31 says God saw all He made was very good, Genesis 1:27 says God created man in His image, and Ephesians 4:24 says man was created in true righteousness and holiness.

before.question: Did God, then, create man so wicked and perverse?
before.answer: No, on the contrary, God created man good and in His image, that is, in true righteousness and holiness, so that he might rightly know God His Creator, heartily love Him, and live with Him in eternal blessedness to praise and glorify Him.
before.right: No. God created man good and in His image in righteousness and holiness to know Him eternally

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Righteousness comes through faith in Jesus Christ, not works of the law (Rom 3:22; Gal 2:16), and in Christ we become the righteousness of God (2 Cor 5:21). The fuller imputation wording is drawn from these and the other proof texts.

before.question: How are you righteous before God?
before.answer: Only by true faith in Jesus Christ. Although my conscience accuses me that I have grievously sinned against all God's commandments, have never kept any of them, and am still inclined to all evil, yet God, without any merit of my own, out of mere grace, imputes to me the perfect satisfaction, righteousness, and holiness of Christ. He grants these to me as if I had never had nor committed any sin, and as if I myself had accomplished all the obedience which Christ has rendered for me, if only I accept this gift with a believing heart.
before.right: Only by faith in Christ; God imputes Christ's satisfaction and righteousness to me as though I never sinned.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Paul rejects his own righteousness and receives the righteousness from God through faith in Christ, and Christ himself is our righteousness (1 Cor 1:30). The answer's "faith only" is drawn from this contrast.

before.question: Why do you say that you are righteous only by faith?
before.answer: Not that I am acceptable to God on account of the worthiness of my faith, for only the satisfaction, righteousness, and holiness of Christ is my righteousness before God. I can receive this righteousness and make it mine in no other way than by faith only.
before.right: Not because faith itself is righteous, but Christ's satisfaction and righteousness are mine; I receive them by faith only.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Galatians 3:10 requires continuing to do everything written in the law, so perfect obedience is needed, while Isaiah 64:6 says even our righteous acts are like filthy rags, showing our works are defiled.

before.question: But why can our good works not be our righteousness before God, or at least a part of it?
before.answer: Because the righteousness which can stand before God's judgment must be absolutely perfect and in complete agreement with the law of God, whereas even our best works in this life are all imperfect and defiled with sin.
before.right: God's law requires perfect righteousness; our best works are imperfect and defiled.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Romans 11:6 says that if something is by grace it is no longer by works, so grace excludes earning. Luke 17:10 says faithful servants have only done their duty, so their service earns no reward.

before.question: But do our good works earn nothing, even though God promises to reward them in this life and the next?
before.answer: This reward is not earned; it is a gift of grace.
before.right: This reward is not earned; it is a gift of grace.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: John 15:5 says those who remain in Christ bear much fruit, and Matthew 7:18 says a good tree cannot bear bad fruit, so union with Christ yields fruit.

before.question: Does this teaching not make people careless and wicked?
before.answer: No. It is impossible that those grafted into Christ by true faith should not bring forth fruits of thankfulness.
before.right: No. It is impossible that those grafted into Christ by true faith should not bring forth fruits of thankfulness.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Faith comes by hearing the word of Christ (Rom 10:17), is the gift of God (Eph 2:8), and is born of the Spirit (John 3:5). The verses shown do not speak of sacraments strengthening faith.

before.question: Since then faith alone makes us share in Christ and all His benefits, where does this faith come from?
before.answer: From the Holy Spirit, who works it in our hearts by the preaching of the gospel, and strengthens it by the use of the sacraments.
before.right: From the Holy Spirit, who works it by the gospel and strengthens it through the sacraments.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Romans 4:11 calls circumcision a sign and seal, Genesis 17:11 a sign of the covenant instituted by God, and Matthew 26:28 and Hebrews 10:10 tie the signs to forgiveness through Christ's once-for-all sacrifice.

before.question: What are the sacraments?
before.answer: The sacraments are holy, visible signs and seals. They were instituted by God so that by their use He might the more fully declare and seal to us the promise of the gospel. And this is the promise: that God graciously grants us forgiveness of sins and everlasting life because of the one sacrifice of Christ accomplished on the cross.
before.right: Holy visible signs and seals instituted by God declaring and sealing forgiveness and eternal life through Christ's one sacrifice.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Hebrews 10:10 names the one sacrifice of Christ's body once for all; Romans 6:3 and 1 Corinthians 11:26 tie baptism and the Lord's Supper to His death; Ephesians 1:13 links hearing the gospel with being sealed by the Spirit.

before.question: According to the Heidelberg Catechism, what does the Holy Spirit teach us in the gospel and assure us by the sacraments that our entire salvation rests on?
before.answer: Christ's one sacrifice for us on the cross. The Holy Spirit teaches this in the gospel and assures us of it by the sacraments.
before.right: Christ's one sacrifice for us on the cross

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Christ commands baptism in Matthew 28:19 and institutes the Lord's Supper in 1 Corinthians 11:24-25. The count of two follows from these two institutions, though the verses do not use the word "sacrament" or state the number.

before.question: How many sacraments has Christ instituted in the new covenant?
before.answer: Two: holy baptism and the holy supper.
before.right: Two: holy baptism and the holy supper.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Acts 2:38 links baptism with forgiveness of sins and the Spirit; Hebrews 9:14 says Christ's blood purifies the conscience; Hebrews 10:22 pairs washing with pure water with cleansing from a guilty conscience.

before.question: How does holy baptism signify and seal to you that the one sacrifice of Christ on the cross benefits you?
before.answer: In this way: Christ instituted this outward washing and with it gave the promise that, as surely as water washes away the dirt from the body, so certainly His blood and Spirit wash away the impurity of my soul, that is, all my sins.
before.right: Water in baptism washes dirt as His blood and Spirit wash away all my sins, Christ's promise at His institution.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Romans 5:12 and 5:19 say sin entered through one man and that the many were made sinners through Adam's disobedience; Psalm 51:5 says the psalmist was sinful when conceived. Genesis 3 narrates the fall.

before.question: From where, then, did man's depraved nature come?
before.answer: From the fall and disobedience of our first parents, Adam and Eve, in Paradise, for there our nature became so corrupt that we are all conceived and born in sin.
before.right: From the fall and disobedience of Adam and Eve, by which our nature became corrupt and sinful

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Ephesians 1:7 gives forgiveness of trespasses through Christ's blood and God's grace. Ezekiel 36:26, 1 Corinthians 6:11 and Romans 6:4 show the Spirit renewing and sanctifying believers and bringing newness of life.

before.question: What does it mean to be washed with Christ's blood and Spirit?
before.answer: To be washed with Christ's blood means to receive forgiveness of sins from God, through grace, because of Christ's blood, poured out for us in His sacrifice on the cross. To be washed with His Spirit means to be renewed by the Holy Spirit and sanctified to be members of Christ, so that more and more we become dead to sin and lead a holy and blameless life.
before.right: Christ's blood washes away sins through grace; His Spirit renews and sanctifies us to live holy.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: The answer points to Christ's baptismal commission and to passages calling baptism a washing: Titus 3:5 speaks of the washing of new birth and renewal by the Spirit, and Acts 22:16 of washing sins away.

before.question: Where has Christ promised that He will wash us with His blood and Spirit as surely as we are washed with the water of baptism?
before.answer: In the institution of baptism, where He says: “Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” and “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned.” This promise is repeated where Scripture speaks of baptism as the washing of new birth and the washing away of sins.
before.right: In the institution of baptism, a promise repeated where Scripture speaks of the washing of new birth

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: 1 John 1:7 says the blood of Jesus cleanses from all sin; 1 Corinthians 6:11 says believers were washed by the Spirit; 1 Peter 3:21 says baptism is not the removal of dirt from the body.

before.question: Does this outward washing with water itself wash away sins?
before.answer: No, only the blood of Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit cleanse us from all sins.
before.right: No, only the blood of Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit cleanse us from all sins.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Titus 3:5 calls baptism the washing of new birth and renewal by the Spirit, Acts 22:16 says baptism washes sins away, and 1 Peter 3:21 calls the water a pledge of a clear conscience.

before.question: Why does the Holy Spirit call baptism the washing of new birth and renewal, and the washing away of sins?
before.answer: God speaks in this way for a good reason. He wants to teach us that the blood and Spirit of Christ remove our sins just as water takes away dirt from the body. But, even more important, He wants to assure us by this divine pledge and sign that we are as truly cleansed from our sins spiritually as we are bodily washed with water.
before.right: God teaches blood and Spirit remove sins like water removes dirt, and assures us we're truly cleansed spiritually as bodily.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Acts 2:39 says the promise belongs to believers' children, Genesis 17:7 makes the covenant with descendants, and Colossians 2:11-12 links baptism with circumcision as the sign of the covenant.

before.question: Should infants, too, be baptized?
before.answer: Yes. Infants as well as adults belong to God's covenant and congregation. Through Christ's blood the redemption from sin and the Holy Spirit, who works faith, are promised to them no less than to adults. Therefore, by baptism, as sign of the covenant, they must be grafted into the Christian church and distinguished from the children of unbelievers. This was done in the old covenant by circumcision, in place of which baptism was instituted in the new covenant.
before.right: Yes, infants belong to God's covenant and receive redemption and Spirit; baptism grafts them into the church replacing circumcision.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Christ commands eating and drinking in remembrance of Him, His body is given and broken for you, His blood poured out for you, and whoever eats His flesh and drinks His blood has eternal life.

before.question: How does the Lord's Supper signify and seal to you that you share in Christ's one sacrifice on the cross and in all His gifts?
before.answer: In this way: Christ has commanded me and all believers to eat of this broken bread and drink of this cup in remembrance of Him. With this command He gave these promises: First, as surely as I see with my eyes the bread of the Lord broken for me and the cup given to me, so surely was His body offered for me and His blood poured out for me on the cross. Second, as surely as I receive from the hand of the minister and taste with my mouth the bread and the cup of the Lord as sure signs of Christ's body and blood, so surely does He Himself nourish and refresh my soul to everlasting life with His crucified body and shed blood.
before.right: As surely as I receive bread and cup, so surely Christ was offered for me and nourishes my soul.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: John 6:35 equates coming to Christ and believing with never hungering or thirsting; John 6:56 says eating and drinking means remaining in Christ, and 1 John 4:13 ties that abiding to the Spirit.

before.question: What does it mean to eat the crucified body of Christ and to drink His shed blood?
before.answer: First, to accept with a believing heart all the suffering and the death of Christ, and so receive forgiveness of sins and life eternal. Second, to be united more and more to His sacred body through the Holy Spirit, who lives both in Christ and in us. Therefore, although Christ is in heaven and we are on earth, yet we are flesh of His flesh and bone of His bones, and we forever live and are governed by one Spirit, as the members of our body are by one soul.
before.right: To accept Christ's suffering and death for forgiveness and be united with His body through the Spirit.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: The answer is the institution of the Lord's Supper, where Christ says of the bread and cup, "This is My body" and "This cup is the new covenant in My blood," and 1 Corinthians 10:16-17 repeats it as participation in His body and blood.

before.question: Where has Christ promised that He will nourish and refresh believers with His body and blood as surely as they eat of this broken bread and drink of this cup?
before.answer: In the institution of the Lord's Supper: "The Lord Jesus, on the night He was betrayed, took bread, and when He had given thanks, He broke it and said, 'This is My body, which is for you; do this in remembrance of Me.' In the same way, after supper He took the cup, saying, 'This cup is the new covenant in My blood; do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of Me.' For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until He comes." Paul repeats this promise: "Is not the cup of blessing that we bless a participation in the blood of Christ? And is not the bread that we break a participation in the body of Christ? Because there is one loaf, we who are many are one body; for we all partake of the one loaf."
before.right: At the institution of the Lord's Supper, and in Paul's words on sharing in Christ's body and blood.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Scripture never states the bread is not changed. It is taught: Christ calls the bread His body (Matt 26:26), Paul calls it bread and a participation in the body (1 Cor 10:16), and Peter says the water symbolizes baptism (1 Pet 3:21).

before.question: Are then the bread and wine changed into the real body and blood of Christ?
before.answer: No. Just as the water of baptism is not changed into the blood of Christ and is not the washing away of sins itself but is simply God's sign and pledge, so also the bread in the Lord's supper does not become the body of Christ itself, although it is called Christ's body in keeping with the nature and usage of sacraments.
before.right: No. Water isn't changed to blood in baptism; bread isn't changed to body in supper but is called so sacramentally.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Scripture calls Christ's flesh real food and His blood real drink (John 6:55), speaks of sharing in His body and blood (1 Cor 10:16), and says we are united with Him in His death (Rom 6:5).

before.question: Why then does Christ call the bread His body and the cup His blood, or the new covenant in His blood, and why does Paul speak of a participation in the body and blood of Christ?
before.answer: Christ speaks in this way for a good reason: He wants to teach us by His supper that as bread and wine sustain us in this temporal life, so His crucified body and shed blood are true food and drink for our souls to eternal life. But, even more important, He wants to assure us by this visible sign and pledge, first, that through the working of the Holy Spirit we share in His true body and blood as surely as we receive with our mouth these holy signs in remembrance of Him, and, second, that all His suffering and obedience are as certainly ours as if we personally had suffered and paid for our sins.
before.right: Bread nourishes bodies as His body nourishes souls eternally; by Spirit we truly share in Him and His suffering becomes ours.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Gen 6:5 says every inclination of man's heart is evil all the time, Jer 13:23 says people cannot do good, and John 3:5 says no one enters God's kingdom unless born of water and the Spirit.

before.question: But are we so corrupt that we are totally unable to do any good and inclined to all evil?
before.answer: Yes, unless we are regenerated by the Spirit of God.
before.right: Yes, unless we are regenerated by the Spirit of God.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Scripture teaches Christ offered one sacrifice for all time, so no further offering is needed, and that He sits at God's right hand in heaven, where He is worshipped in spirit and truth. The verses never mention the papal mass, so that description is the catechism's judgment.

before.question: What difference is there between the Lord's supper and the papal mass?
before.answer: The Lord's supper testifies to us, first, that we have complete forgiveness of all our sins through the one sacrifice of Jesus Christ, which He Himself accomplished on the cross once for all; and, second, that through the Holy Spirit we are grafted into Christ, who with His true body is now in heaven at the right hand of the Father, and this is where He wants to be worshipped. But the mass teaches, first, that the living and the dead do not have forgiveness of sins through the suffering of Christ unless He is still offered for them daily by the priests; and, second, that Christ is bodily present in the form of bread and wine, and there is to be worshipped. Therefore the mass is basically nothing but a denial of the one sacrifice and suffering of Jesus Christ, and an accursed idolatry.
before.right: Supper witnesses complete forgiveness through Christ's one sacrifice; mass wrongly teaches daily re-offering and worship of Christ bodily present in bread.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Paul tells each person to examine himself before eating the bread and drinking the cup, and warns that whoever eats without recognizing the body eats and drinks judgment on himself.

before.question: Who are to come to the table of the Lord?
before.answer: Those who are truly displeased with themselves because of their sins and yet trust that these are forgiven them and that their remaining weakness is covered by the suffering and death of Christ, and who also desire more and more to strengthen their faith and amend their life. But hypocrites and those who do not repent eat and drink judgment upon themselves.
before.right: Those displeased with their sins who trust Christ's death covers them and want to strengthen faith and amend life.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Paul tells the church not to associate with or even eat with a professing brother living in open sin, and to expel such a wicked man; Psalm 50:16 rebukes the wicked who recite God's covenant with their lips.

before.question: Are those also to be admitted to the Lord's Supper who by their confession and life show that they are unbelieving and ungodly?
before.answer: No, for then God's covenant would be profaned and His wrath kindled against the whole congregation. The church must exclude such persons by the keys of the kingdom of heaven until they amend their lives.
before.right: No. The covenant would be profaned and God's wrath kindled. The church must exclude them by ecclesiastical discipline.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Matthew 16:19 gives the keys of the kingdom and binding and loosing. John 20:21-23 has Christ sending the disciples and giving authority to forgive or withhold forgiveness, which the answer draws out as preaching and church discipline.

before.question: What are the keys of the kingdom of heaven?
before.answer: The preaching of the holy gospel and church discipline. By these two the kingdom of heaven is opened to believers and closed to unbelievers.
before.right: Gospel preaching and church discipline. These open the kingdom to believers and close it to unbelievers.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Christ sends the disciples and says forgiven sins are forgiven when they are forgiven (John 20:21-23). The wrath of God remains on whoever rejects the Son (John 3:36). Together they teach the answer's two sides.

before.question: How is the kingdom of heaven opened and closed by the preaching of the gospel?
before.answer: According to the command of Christ, the kingdom of heaven is opened when it is proclaimed and publicly testified to each and every believer that God has really forgiven all their sins for the sake of Christ's merits, as often as they by true faith accept the promise of the gospel. The kingdom of heaven is closed when it is proclaimed and testified to all unbelievers and hypocrites that the wrath of God and eternal condemnation rest on them as long as they do not repent. According to this testimony of the gospel, God will judge both in this life and in the life to come.
before.right: It opens by proclaiming God's forgiveness to believers and closes by proclaiming His wrath on unrepentant unbelievers.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Matthew 18:15-18 gives the stages of brotherly admonition, reporting to the church, and binding and loosing; 1 Corinthians 5:11-13 gives non-association and expulsion; 2 Corinthians 2:6-8 gives restoration after repentance. "Elders" and "forbidden the sacraments" are inferred, not stated.

before.question: How is the kingdom of heaven closed and opened by church discipline?
before.answer: According to the command of Christ, people who call themselves Christians but show themselves to be unchristian in doctrine or life are first repeatedly admonished in a brotherly manner. If they do not give up their errors or wickedness, they are reported to the church, that is, to the elders. If they do not heed also their admonitions, they are forbidden the use of the sacraments, and they are excluded by the elders from the Christian congregation, and by God Himself from the kingdom of Christ. They are again received as members of Christ and of the church when they promise and show real amendment.
before.right: Unchristian members are admonished, reported to elders, forbidden sacraments, and excluded. They're received back when they show real amendment.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Believers offer their bodies as living sacrifices and are transformed by renewed minds; their good deeds let others see and glorify God; practicing these things makes their calling sure.

before.question: Since we have been delivered from our misery by grace alone through Christ, without any merit of our own, why must we yet do good works?
before.answer: Because Christ, having redeemed us by His blood, also renews us by His Holy Spirit to be His image, so that with our whole life we may show ourselves thankful to God for His benefits, and He may be praised by us. Further, that we ourselves may be assured of our faith by its fruits, and that by our godly walk of life we may win our neighbours for Christ.
before.right: Show thankfulness to God and praise Him; assure ourselves of faith by its fruits; win neighbors to Christ by godly living.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Paul says the wicked, including the sexually immoral, idolaters, adulterers, thieves, the greedy, drunkards, and verbal abusers, will not inherit the kingdom of God. Galatians 5:21 says the same of those who practice such things.

before.question: Can those be saved who do not turn to God from their ungrateful and impenitent walk of life?
before.answer: By no means. Scripture says that no unchaste person, idolater, adulterer, thief, greedy person, drunkard, slanderer, robber, or the like shall inherit the kingdom of God.
before.right: By no means. No unchaste person, idolater, adulterer, thief, greedy person, drunkard, slanderer, or robber shall inherit God's kingdom.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Colossians 3:5 says to put to death the components of the earthly nature, and 3:10 says to put on the new self being renewed. That matches dying of the old nature and new life.

before.question: What is the true repentance or conversion of man?
before.answer: It is the dying of the old nature and the coming to life of the new.
before.right: It is the dying of the old nature and the coming to life of the new.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: David confesses that he has sinned against God, and 2 Corinthians 7:10 speaks of godly sorrow that leads to repentance. Romans 8:13 urges putting to death the deeds of the body.

before.question: What is the dying of the old nature?
before.answer: It is to grieve with heartfelt sorrow that we have offended God by our sin, and more and more to hate it and flee from it.
before.right: To grieve with heartfelt sorrow that we offended God by sin, and increasingly to hate and flee from it.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: God made everything very good (Gen 1:31). The woman ate the forbidden fruit (Gen 3:6), the devil is a liar and murderer (John 8:44), and through one man's disobedience sin and death passed to all (Rom 5:12, 5:19).

before.question: Is God, then, not unjust by requiring in His law what man cannot do?
before.answer: No, for God so created man that he was able to do it. But man, at the instigation of the devil, in deliberate disobedience robbed himself and all his descendants of these gifts.
before.right: No. God created man able to obey. Man's disobedience robbed all descendants of these gifts

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Psalm 51:12 asks for restored joy in God's salvation and a willing spirit; Romans 14:17 names joy in the Holy Spirit; Ephesians 2:10 says believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.

before.question: What is the coming to life of the new nature?
before.answer: It is a heartfelt joy in God through Christ, and a love and delight to live according to the will of God in all good works.
before.right: Heartfelt joy in God through Christ, and love and delight to live according to God's will in all good works.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Romans 14:23 says what is not from faith is sin; Leviticus 18:4 requires keeping God's judgments; 1 Corinthians 10:31 directs all to God's glory; Matthew 15:9 rejects worship taught as men's precepts.

before.question: But what are good works?
before.answer: Only those which are done out of true faith, in accordance with the law of God, and to His glory, and not those based on our own opinion or on precepts of men.
before.right: Works from true faith, according to God's law, to His glory, not based on our opinions or human precepts.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: The answer is the text of the Ten Commandments, which Exodus 20:1-17 gives as the words God spoke: "And God spoke all these words," followed by the commandments.

before.question: What is the law of the LORD?
before.answer: And God spoke all these words: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. (1) You shall have no other gods before Me. (2) You shall not make for yourself an idol in the form of anything in the heavens above, on the earth below, or in the waters beneath. You shall not bow down to them or worship them; for I, the LORD your God, am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on their children to the third and fourth generations of those who hate Me, but showing loving devotion to a thousand generations of those who love Me and keep My commandments. (3) You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain, for the LORD will not leave anyone unpunished who takes His name in vain. (4) Remember the Sabbath day by keeping it holy. Six days you shall labor and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God, on which you must not do any work—neither you, nor your son or daughter, nor your manservant or maidservant or livestock, nor the foreigner within your gates. For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth and the sea and all that is in them, but on the seventh day He rested. Therefore the LORD blessed the Sabbath day and set it apart as holy. (5) Honor your father and mother, so that your days may be long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you. (6) You shall not murder. (7) You shall not commit adultery. (8) You shall not steal. (9) You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor. (10) You shall not covet your neighbor’s house. You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, or his manservant or maidservant, or his ox or donkey, or anything that belongs to your neighbor.”
before.right: The Ten Commandments of God revealed to Moses at Mount Sinai.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Jesus sets the law in two parts: love the Lord your God first and greatest, and love your neighbor as yourself, with all the Law hanging on these two.

before.question: How are these commandments divided?
before.answer: Into two parts. The first teaches us how to live in relation to God; the second, what duties we owe our neighbor.
before.right: Into two parts: first, how to live toward God; second, our duties toward our neighbor.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: The answer is drawn from the proof texts: flee idolatry and witchcraft (Deut 18, 1 Cor 10:14), worship no creature (Rev 22:8-9), worship God alone (Matt 4:10), know, trust, and love Him (John 17:3, Jer 17:7, Deut 6:5), and expect good from Him (Jas 1:17).

before.question: What does the LORD require in the first commandment?
before.answer: That for the sake of my very salvation I avoid and flee all idolatry, witchcraft, superstition, and prayer to saints or to other creatures. Further, that I rightly come to know the only true God, trust in Him alone, submit to Him with all humility and patience, expect all good from Him only, and love, fear, and honor Him with all my heart. In short, that I forsake all creatures rather than do the least thing against His will.
before.right: Flee idolatry, trust the only God alone, love and fear Him, and forsake all creatures rather than disobey Him.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Only the LORD made the heavens, while other gods are idols (1 Chr 16:26). Idols are trusted and made (Ps 31:6; Hab 2:18), and a god can be one's belly (Phil 3:19).

before.question: What is idolatry?
before.answer: Idolatry is having or inventing something in which to put our trust instead of, or in addition to, the only true God who has revealed Himself in His Word.
before.right: Having or inventing something to trust in instead of or along with the only true God revealed in His Word.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Israel saw no form of God at Horeb, so they must not make an idol in the form of man, beast, bird, creeping thing, or fish. The prohibition targets idols made to be worshipped.

before.question: May we then not make any image at all?
before.answer: No. God cannot and may not be visibly portrayed in any way. Creatures may be portrayed, but God forbids us to make or have any images of them in order to worship them or to serve God through them.
before.right: No. God cannot be visibly portrayed. Creatures may be portrayed, but forbidden for worship or serving God through them.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:heidelbe.note: Habakkuk 2:18-19 calls idols teachers of lies that cannot speak or give guidance, while Romans 10:14 and 17 say faith comes through hearing the preached word of Christ, which supports the answer.

before.question: But may images not be tolerated in the churches as "books for the laity"?
before.answer: No, for we should not be wiser than God. He wants His people to be taught not by means of dumb images but by the living preaching of His Word.
before.right: No. God wants His people taught by living preaching of His Word, not by dumb images.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:keachs_c.note: Matthew 28:19 names the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together in one name, John 10:30 says the Father and Son are one, and Acts 5:3-4 equates lying to the Spirit with lying to God.

before.question: How many persons are there in the Godhead?
before.answer: There are three persons in the Godhead, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one God, the same in essence, equal in power and glory.
before.right: Three persons in the Godhead—Father, Son, Spirit—one God in essence and power

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:keachs_c.note: Believers gather as an assembly across ages (Acts 7:38), receive baptism and teaching and break bread together (Acts 2:41-42; 20:7), and are equipped by teachers for building up the body (Eph 4:11-12).

before.question: What is the visible church?
before.answer: The visible church is the organized society of professing believers, in all ages and places, wherein the Gospel is truly preached and the ordinances of Baptism and the Lord's Supper rightly administered.
before.right: The organized society of professing believers where the Gospel is truly preached and ordinances rightly administered

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:keachs_c.note: Matthew 6:11 gives the request for daily bread. Proverbs 30:8 asks for neither poverty nor riches, a competent portion. First Timothy 4:4-5 says God's creation is good, to be received with thanksgiving and sanctified by prayer, which matches enjoying His blessing.

before.question: What do we pray for in the fourth petition?
before.answer: In the fourth petition, which is, "Give us this day our daily bread," we pray that of God's free gift, we may receive a competent portion of the good things of this life and enjoy His blessing with them.
before.right: We pray for a competent portion of life's good things and God's blessing

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:keachs_c.note: Matthew 6:12 asks God to forgive our debts; Psalm 51:1 pleads for blotted-out transgressions. Matthew 6:14-15 and Ephesians 4:32 tie God's forgiveness to forgiving others, with "in Christ" God forgave us.

before.question: What do we pray for in the fifth petition?
before.answer: In the fifth petition, which is, "And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors," we pray that God, for Christ's sake, would freely pardon all our sins; which we are the rather encouraged to ask, because by His grace we are enabled from the heart to forgive others.
before.right: We pray God would freely pardon our sins, encouraged because He enables us to forgive

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:keachs_c.note: Matthew 6:13 gives the petition: "lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one." The answer restates this, with the proof texts (Matt 26:41, 1 Cor 10:13, John 17:15) supporting the keeping and the deliverance.

before.question: What do we pray for in the sixth petition?
before.answer: In the sixth petition, which is, "And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one," we pray that God would either keep us from being tempted to sin, or support and deliver us when we are tempted.
before.right: We pray God would either keep us from temptation or support us when tempted

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:keachs_c.note: Genesis 1:1 shows God's work of creation, and Acts 14:17 shows His providence, as He gives rain and fruitful seasons. Together these teach the answer, though the verses do not use the word "decrees."

before.question: How does God execute His decrees?
before.answer: God executes His decrees in the works of creation and providence.
before.right: God executes His decrees in the works of creation and providence.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:keachs_c.note: Hebrews 11:3 says the universe was formed at God's command, not from what is visible; Exodus 20:11 gives the six days; Genesis 1:31 says everything was very good.

before.question: What is the work of creation?
before.answer: The work of creation is God's making all things of nothing, by the Word of His power, in the space of six days, and all very good.
before.right: God's making all things from nothing by the word of His power.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:keachs_c.note: Genesis 1:27 gives male and female in God's image, Genesis 1:28 gives dominion, Ephesians 4:24 gives righteousness and holiness, and Colossians 3:10 gives knowledge after the Creator's image.

before.question: How did God create man?
before.answer: God created man male and female, after His own image, in knowledge, righteousness, and holiness, with dominion over the creatures.
before.right: God created man male and female in His image, in knowledge and holiness.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:keachs_c.note: Hebrews 1:3 says the Son upholds all things by His powerful word, Psalm 103:19 says His kingdom rules over all, and Matthew 10:29-30 shows He governs even sparrows and the hairs of our heads.

before.question: What are God's works of providence?
before.answer: God's works of providence are His most holy, wise, and powerful preserving and governing all His creatures, and all their actions.
before.right: God's most holy, wise, and powerful preserving and governing all creatures.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:keachs_c.note: Genesis 3:6 records the first pair eating the forbidden fruit. Ecclesiastes 7:29 says God made men upright but they sought out many schemes, so they left their created state by sinning.

before.question: Did our first parents continue in the estate wherein they were created?
before.answer: Our first parents, being left to the freedom of their own will, fell from the estate wherein they were created, by sinning against God.
before.right: Our first parents fell from the estate wherein they were created by sinning against God

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:keachs_c.note: 1 John 3:4 says sin is lawlessness, which is the transgression of God's law the answer names. Romans 5:13 supports this by showing sin is reckoned only where there is law.

before.question: What is sin?
before.answer: Sin is any want of conformity unto, or transgression of, the law of God.
before.right: Any want of conformity unto, or transgression of, God's law

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:keachs_c.note: First Corinthians 10:31 commands doing all to God's glory, and Psalm 73:25-26 speaks of desiring God alone and God as one's portion forever, which supports enjoying Him forever.

before.question: What is the chief end of man?
before.answer: Man's chief end is to glorify God and to enjoy Him forever.
before.right: Man's chief end is to glorify God and to enjoy Him forever

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:keachs_c.note: Romans 5:12 and 5:18-19 teach that through one man's trespass death passed to all men and many were made sinners. The word "covenant" with Adam is not stated in these verses.

before.question: Did all mankind fall in Adam's first transgression?
before.answer: The covenant being made with Adam, not only for himself but for his posterity, all mankind, descending from him by ordinary generation, sinned in him, and fell with him in his first transgression.
before.right: All mankind, descending from Adam, sinned in him and fell with him

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:keachs_c.note: Luke 1:31-35 has the virgin Mary conceive by the Holy Spirit; Hebrews 2:14 says He shared flesh and blood; Matthew 26:38 shows a soul; Hebrews 4:15 says He was without sin.

before.question: How did Christ, being the Son of God, become man?
before.answer: Christ, the Son of God became man by taking to himself a true body and a reasonable soul; being conceived by the power of the Holy Spirit in the womb of the Virgin Mary and born of her, yet without sin.
before.right: Christ took a true body and soul, conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of Mary

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:keachs_c.note: First Corinthians 6:11 says those called were justified and sanctified in Christ's name, and Galatians 3:26 says they are sons of God through faith, which is adoption. The answer's wording about other accompanying benefits is a general summary.

before.question: What benefits do they that are effectually called, partake of in this life?
before.answer: They that are effectually called, do in this life partake of justification, adoption, sanctification, and the several benefits which in this life do either accompany or flow from them.
before.right: They partake of justification, adoption, sanctification, and the several benefits which accompany or flow from them

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:keachs_c.note: Ephesians 1:5-6 says God predestined us for adoption as sons by the good pleasure of His will, freely given by grace. John 1:12 gives the right to become children, and Romans 8:17 says we are heirs with Christ.

before.question: What is adoption?
before.answer: Adoption is an act of God's free grace, whereby we are received into the number, and have a right to all the privileges of the sons of God.
before.right: An act of God's free grace whereby we are received as sons of God

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:keachs_c.note: Romans 5:1-5 gives peace with God, joy and hope, and God's love poured out by the Spirit; Romans 14:17 names joy in the Holy Spirit; Proverbs 4:18 pictures growing light; 1 Peter 1:5 says believers are shielded for salvation.

before.question: What are the benefits which in this life do accompany or flow from justification, adoption, and sanctification?
before.answer: The benefits which in this life do accompany or flow from justification, adoption, and sanctification, are, assurance of God's love, peace of conscience, joy in the Holy Spirit, increase of grace, and perseverance therein to the end.
before.right: Assurance of God's love, peace of conscience, joy in the Holy Spirit, increase of grace, and perseverance

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:keachs_c.note: Ecclesiastes 12:13 says that to fear God and keep His commandments is the whole duty of man, which matches the answer that God requires obedience to His revealed will.

before.question: What is the duty which God requires of man?
before.answer: The duty which God requires of man, is obedience to His revealed will.
before.right: God requires man's obedience to His revealed will

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:keachs_c.note: Romans 2:15 says the work of the law is written on human hearts, and Romans 5:13-14 shows a law and sin in force from Adam to Moses, so a law was given to man before Sinai.

before.question: What did God at first reveal to man for the rule of his obedience?
before.answer: The rule which God at first revealed to man for his obedience was the moral law.
before.right: The moral law God revealed to man for his obedience

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:keachs_c.note: Deuteronomy 10:4 says the LORD wrote the Ten Commandments on the tablets, so the answer that the moral law is comprehended in them follows from that verse. Matthew 19:17-18 points the same way.

before.question: Where is the moral law summarily comprehended?
before.answer: The moral law is summarily comprehended in the Ten Commandments.
before.right: The moral law is summarily comprehended in the Ten Commandments.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:keachs_c.note: Psalm 19:7-9 describes the Lord's law as perfect, reviving the soul and pure. Believers receive it as God's word, at work in them (1 Thess 2:13), and the Spirit's anointing teaches them (1 John 2:27).

before.question: How do we know that the Bible is the Word of God?
before.answer: The Bible evidences itself to be God's Word by the heavenliness of its doctrine, the unity of its parts, its power to convert sinners and to edify saints; but the Spirit of God only, bearing witness by and with the Scriptures in our hearts, is able fully to persuade us that the Bible is the Word of God.
before.right: The Spirit of God bearing witness in our hearts persuades us the Bible is God's Word

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:keachs_c.note: Exodus 20:3 gives the answer word for word: "You shall have no other gods before Me." It is the first of the commandments given after God's opening words in Exodus 20:2.

before.question: Which is the first commandment?
before.answer: The first commandment is, "You shall have no other gods before Me."
before.right: The first commandment is, "You shall have no other gods before Me."

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:keachs_c.note: God is Spirit (John 4:24), everlasting (Ps 90:2), with no change (James 1:17), of unlimited understanding and power (Ps 147:5), holy (Rev 4:8), and good, just, and faithful (Exod 34:6-7).

before.question: What is God?
before.answer: God is a Spirit, infinite, eternal, and unchangeable in His being, wisdom, power, holiness, justice, goodness and truth.
before.right: A Spirit, infinite, eternal, and unchangeable in His being, wisdom, power, holiness, justice, goodness and truth.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:keachs_c.note: The law is perfect and righteous and gives wisdom and warning (Ps 19:7-11). It shows God's will (Rom 12:2), brings awareness of sin (Rom 3:20), leads us to Christ (Gal 3:24), and is laid on the lawless (1 Tim 1:9).

before.question: What then is the purpose of the law since the fall?
before.answer: The purpose of the law, since the fall, is to reveal the perfect righteousness of God, that His people may know His will for their lives, and the ungodly, being convicted of their sin, may be restrained thereby and brought to Christ for salvation.
before.right: To reveal God's perfect righteousness so His people know His will and the ungodly are convicted

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:keachs_c.note: Jesus says Pilate has sin, but the one who handed Him over is "guilty of greater sin," so some sins are greater than others before God.

before.question: Are all transgressions of the law equally heinous?
before.answer: Some sins in themselves and by reason of several aggravations, are more heinous in the sight of God than others.
before.right: Some sins, by reason of aggravations, are more heinous in God's sight

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:keachs_c.note: Scripture teaches faith as receiving Christ (John 1:12), trusting in Jesus Christ for justification apart from works (Galatians 2:16), and salvation through faith as God's gift of grace (Ephesians 2:8).

before.question: What is faith in Jesus Christ?
before.answer: Faith in Jesus Christ is a saving grace, whereby we receive and rest upon Him alone for salvation, as He is offered to us in the Gospel.
before.right: A saving grace whereby we receive and rest upon Christ alone for salvation

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:keachs_c.note: Christ commands baptism (Matt 28:19) and institutes the Supper, with bread as His body and the cup as His covenant blood poured out for forgiveness (Matt 26:26-28). Baptism pictures burial and resurrection with Christ (Rom 6:4). The "other ordinances" contrast is not stated.

before.question: Wherein do Baptism and the Lord's Supper differ from the other ordinances of God?
before.answer: Baptism and the Lord's Supper differ from the other ordinances of God in that they were specially instituted by Christ to represent and apply to believers the benefits of the new covenant by visible and outward signs.
before.right: Specially instituted by Christ to represent and apply to believers benefits of the new covenant

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:puritan_.note: Scripture is God-breathed and useful for instruction and training, so that the man of God is fully equipped for every good work. The verses teach Scripture as the sufficient guide for living to God's glory; "only" and "enjoy" are not stated.

before.question: What rule has God given to direct us how we may glorify him?
before.answer: The Word of God which is contained in the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments is the only rule to direct us how we may glorify God and enjoy him.
before.right: The Word of God in the Scriptures of Old and New Testaments is the only rule to glorify God

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:puritan_.note: Exodus 20:7 gives the wording of the answer word for word. The count to "third" follows from the order of the commandments in Exodus 20, with the verse numbering matching that order.

before.question: Which is the third commandment?
before.answer: You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain, for the LORD will not leave anyone unpunished who takes His name in vain.
before.right: You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:puritan_.note: Exodus 23:13 and Proverbs 30:6 warn against adding to God's words but never mention baptism or infants. The conclusion that infants should not be baptized is church teaching drawn from the absence of a command or example.
creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:puritan_.doubt: The claim that Scripture has no example of infant baptism is disputed, since household baptisms such as 1 Corinthians 1:16 do not say whether children were included.

before.question: Are the infants of such as are professing believers to be baptized?
before.answer: The infants of such as are professing believers are not to be baptized, because there is neither command nor example in the Holy Scriptures for their baptism.
before.right: No; infants are not to be baptized; there is neither command nor example in Scripture

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:puritan_.note: Acts 1:11 says the Jesus taken into heaven will come back, and 1 Thessalonians 2:19 names His coming as the hope and joy of believers.

before.question: What is meant by the words "until He comes," which the apostle Paul uses in reference to the Lord's Supper?
before.answer: They plainly teach us that our Lord Jesus Christ will come a second time; which is the joy and hope of all believers.
before.right: They teach that Jesus Christ will come a second time, which is the joy and hope of believers

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Hebrews 1:5 shows the Father begetting the Son, John 15:26 the Spirit proceeding from the Father, and Galatians 4:6 the Spirit sent as the Son's Spirit. "From all eternity" is a theological gloss not stated in these verses.

before.question: What are the personal properties of the three persons in the Godhead?
before.answer: It is proper to the Father to beget the Son, and to the Son to be begotten of the Father, and to the Holy Spirit to proceed from the Father and the Son from all eternity.
before.right: The Father begets the Son, the Son is begotten of the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from both eternally.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Exodus 20:2 is the preface ("I am the LORD your God..."), 20:3-17 give the commandments, and reasons are annexed in 20:5-7 and 20:11-12 ("for," "so that"), matching the answer.

before.question: What special things are we to consider in the ten commandments?
before.answer: We are to consider, in the ten commandments, the preface, the substance of the commandments themselves, and several reasons annexed to some of them, the more to enforce them.
before.right: Consider the preface, substance of the commandments, and reasons annexed to some to enforce them

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Luke 10:27 gives the answer in nearly the same words: to love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, strength, and mind. The verse does not name the "four commandments," but the content matches.

before.question: What is the sum of the four commandments which contain our duty to God?
before.answer: The sum of the four commandments containing our duty to God is, to love the Lord our God with all our heart, and with all our soul, and with all our strength, and with all our mind.
before.right: Love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, strength, and mind

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: The shown verses condemn atheism (Ps 14:1), idolatry (Jer 2:27-28; Acts 17:23, 29), neglect and forgetfulness of God (Isa 43:22-24; Hos 4:6; Ps 50:21), and being without God (Eph 2:12); the full list is drawn from its proof texts.

before.question: What are the sins forbidden in the first commandment?
before.answer: The sins forbidden in the first commandment are, atheism, in denying or not having a God; Idolatry, in having or worshiping more gods than one, or any with or instead of the true God; the not having and avouching him for God, and our God; the omission or neglect of anything due to him, required in this commandment; ignorance, forgetfulness, misapprehensions, false opinions, unworthy and wicked thoughts of him; bold and curious searching into his secrets; all profaneness, hatred of God; self-love, self-seeking, and all other inordinate and immoderate setting of our mind, will, or affections upon other things, and taking them off from him in whole or in part; vain credulity, unbelief, heresy, misbelief, distrust, despair, incorrigibleness, and insensibleness under judgments, hardness of heart, pride, presumption, carnal security, tempting of God; using unlawful means, and trusting in lawful means; carnal delights and joys; corrupt, blind, and indiscreet zeal; lukewarmness, and deadness in the things of God; estranging ourselves, and apostatizing from God; praying, or giving any religious worship, to saints, angels, or any other creatures; all compacts and consulting with the devil, and hearkening to his suggestions; making men the lords of our faith and conscience; slighting and despising God and his commands; resisting and grieving of his Spirit, discontent and impatience at his dispensations, charging him foolishly for the evils he inflicts on us; and ascribing the praise of any good we either are, have, or can do, to fortune, idols, ourselves, or any other creature.
before.right: Atheism, idolatry, neglect of duty, ignorance, false thoughts of God, profaneness, hatred, self-love, unbelief, despair, pride, tempting God

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: The Word, who is the Son, is called God (John 1:1). Lying to the Holy Spirit is lying to God (Acts 5:4). All things were created through the Son (Col 1:16). Baptism is in the one name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit (Matt 28:19).

before.question: How does it appear that the Son and the Holy Spirit are God equal with the Father?
before.answer: The Scriptures show that the Son and the Holy Spirit are God equal with the Father, ascribing to them such names, attributes, works, and worship as are proper to God only.
before.right: Scripture ascribes to the Son and the Spirit God's proper names, attributes, works, and worship.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Exodus 20:10 charges the head of the household that son, daughter, servants, livestock and the foreigner must not work on the Sabbath. Nehemiah 13:17 rebukes the nobles for profaning it, showing superiors' responsibility and their tendency to hinder others.

before.question: Why is the charge of keeping the sabbath more specially directed to governors of families, and other superiors?
before.answer: The charge of keeping the sabbath is more specially directed to governors of families, and other superiors, because they are bound not only to keep it themselves, but to see that it be observed by all those that are under their charge; and because they are prone ofttimes to hinder them by employments of their own.
before.right: Directed to governors and superiors; they must keep it and ensure those under them observe it and not hinder them

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: The shown verses contain the word "Remember" (Exod 20:8) and tie remembrance to creation and redemption (Exod 20:11, Deut 5:15). The reasons about human forgetfulness, worldly business, and Satan's work are the divines' own reasoning, not stated in these verses.

before.question: Why is the word Remember set in the beginning of the fourth commandment?
before.answer: The word Remember is set in the beginning of the fourth commandment, partly, because of the great benefit of remembering it, we being thereby helped in our preparation to keep it, and, in keeping it, better to keep all the rest of the commandments, and to continue a thankful remembrance of the two great benefits of creation and redemption, which contain a short abridgment of religion; and partly, because we are very ready to forget it, for that there is less light of nature for it, and yet it restraineth our natural liberty in things at other times lawful; that it comes but once in seven days, and many worldly businesses come between, and too often take off our minds from thinking of it, either to prepare for it, or to sanctify it; and that Satan with his instruments much labor to blot out the glory, and even the memory of it, to bring in all irreligion and impiety.
before.right: Remembering helps us keep it and all the commandments, and we are very ready to forget it

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Matthew 22:39 states "Love your neighbor as yourself," and Matthew 7:12 states "do to others as you would have them do to you," the two parts of the answer.

before.question: What is the sum of the six commandments which contain our duty to man?
before.answer: The sum of the six commandments which contain our duty to man is, to love our neighbor as ourselves, and to do to others what we would have them to do to us.
before.right: Love your neighbor as yourself, and do to others as you would have them do to you

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Paul tells Timothy to treat older men as fathers and older women as mothers, Elisha calls Elijah "my father," and Joseph is made a father to Pharaoh. "Father" reaches beyond natural parents to age, gifts, and authority.

before.question: Who are meant by father and mother in the fifth commandment?
before.answer: By father and mother, in the fifth commandment, are meant, not only natural parents, but all superiors in age and gifts; and especially such as, by God's ordinance, are over us in place of authority, whether in family, church, or commonwealth.
before.right: Not only natural parents, but all superiors in age and gifts, especially those in authority in family, church, commonwealth

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Paul was gentle like a nursing mother and treated the Thessalonians as a father treats his children, and Naaman's servants called him "My father" and urged ready obedience.

before.question: Why are superiors styled Father and Mother?
before.answer: Superiors are styled Father and Mother, both to teach them in all duties toward their inferiors, like natural parents, to express love and tenderness to them, according to their several relations; and to work inferiors to a greater willingness and cheerfulness in performing their duties to their superiors, as to their parents.
before.right: Styled Father and Mother to teach superiors to be like parents expressing love and tenderness, making inferiors more willing in duties

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Scripture teaches respect and honor to those owed it, obedience and submission to leaders, prayer for rulers, imitation of those who lead, defense of the king, and submission to masters. Together these match the listed duties.

before.question: What is the honor that inferiors owe to their superiors?
