before.answer: The honor which inferiors owe to their superiors is, all due reverence in heart, word, and behavior; prayer and thanksgiving for them; imitation of their virtues and graces; willing obedience to their lawful commands and counsels; due submission to their corrections; fidelity to, defense and maintenance of their persons and authority, according to their several ranks, and the nature of their places; bearing with their infirmities, and covering them in love, that so they may be an honor to them and to their government.
before.right: Due reverence in heart, word, and behavior; prayer and thanksgiving for them; willing obedience to their lawful commands

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Neglecting parental honor and cursing parents (Matt 15:4-6), Joshua's jealousy (Num 11:28-29), contempt for Saul (1 Sam 10:27), rejecting God's king (1 Sam 8:7), mocking parents (Prov 30:17), and shameful conduct (Prov 19:26) together show the sins listed.

before.question: What are the sins of inferiors against their superiors?
before.answer: The sins of inferiors against their superiors are, all neglect of the duties required toward them; envying at, contempt of, and rebellion against, their persons and places, in their lawful counsels, commands, and corrections; cursing, mocking, and all such refractory and scandalous carriage, as proves a shame and dishonor to them and their government.
before.right: Neglect of duties toward them; envy, contempt, and rebellion against them; cursing, mocking, and scandalous conduct that shames them and their government.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Scripture sets out these superior's duties across several passages: love and prayer (Col 3:19, 1 Sam 12:23), instruction (Eph 6:4), rewarding good and punishing evil (Rom 13:3-4), and protection and provision (Job 29:12-17, 1 Tim 5:8).

before.question: What is required of superiors towards their inferiors?
before.answer: It is required of superiors, according to that power they receive from God, and that relation wherein they stand, to love, pray for, and bless their inferiors; to instruct, counsel, and admonish them; countenancing, commending, and rewarding such as do well; and discountenancing, reproving, and chastising such as do ill; protecting, and providing for them all things necessary for soul and body: and by grave, wise, holy, and exemplary carriage, to procure glory to God, honor to themselves, and so to preserve that authority which God hath put upon them.
before.right: Love, pray for, and instruct inferiors; reward the good, chasten the evil, provide for needs, and set holy examples.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Ephesians 1:4-5 shows God choosing and predestining people before the world's foundation, Romans 9:18 shows His choosing whom He wills, Romans 9:22 shows vessels of wrath, and 1 Timothy 5:21 names elect angels.
creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.doubt: The shown verses speak of elect angels but do not state that other angels were passed by, so that part of the answer is inferred rather than stated.

before.question: What hath God especially decreed concerning angels and men?
before.answer: God, by an eternal and immutable decree, out of his mere love, for the praise of his glorious grace, to be manifested in due time, hath elected some angels to glory; and in Christ hath chosen some men to eternal life, and the means thereof: and also, according to his sovereign power, and the unsearchable counsel of his own will (whereby he extendeth or withholdeth favor as he pleases), hath passed by and foreordained the rest to dishonor and wrath, to be for their sin inflicted, to the praise of the glory of his justice.
before.right: God eternally elected some angels to glory and some men to eternal life in Christ, and foreordained others to wrath.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: The shown verses condemn leaders who feed themselves and neglect their flock, seek their own glory and gain, give unjust or impossible orders, forbid good, provoke children, and fail to restrain wrong. The list follows from these proof texts.

before.question: What are the sins of superiors?
before.answer: The sins of superiors are, besides the neglect of the duties required of them, an inordinate seeking of themselves, their own glory, ease, profit, or pleasure; commanding things unlawful, or not in the power of inferiors to perform; counseling, encouraging, or favoring them in that which is evil; dissuading, discouraging, or discountenancing them in that which is good; correcting them unduly; careless exposing, or leaving them to wrong, temptation, and danger; provoking them to wrath; or any way dishonoring themselves, or lessening their authority, by an unjust, indiscreet, rigorous, or remiss behavior.
before.right: Neglecting their duties, seeking their own glory and ease, commanding unlawful things, encouraging evil, discouraging good, and correcting unduly

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Romans 12:10 calls believers to outdo one another in honor, Philippians 2:3 to count others more important, and Romans 12:15 to rejoice with those who rejoice, with Philippians 2:4 looking to others' interests.

before.question: What are the duties of equals?
before.answer: The duties of equals are, to regard the dignity and worth of each other, in giving honor to go one before another; and to rejoice in each other's gifts and advancement, as their own.
before.right: Regard each other's dignity and worth, give honor, and rejoice in each other's gifts and advancement

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Scripture shows the sins named: Miriam and Aaron dispute Moses' place, Galatians envy one another, Haman grieves at Mordecai's honor, and the disciples argue over who is greatest.

before.question: What are the sins of equals?
before.answer: The sins of equals are, besides the neglect of the duties required, the undervaluing of the worth, envying the gifts, grieving at the advancement or prosperity one of another; and usurping preeminence one over another.
before.right: Neglect of duties, undervaluing worth, envying gifts, grieving at advancement or prosperity, usurping preeminence

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Scripture forbids unlawful killing (Gen 9:6; Num 35:31), anger and hatred (Matt 5:22; 1 John 3:15), neglecting the needy (James 2:15-16), anxious cares (Matt 6:31), harsh words, striking, drunkenness, and oppression.

before.question: What are the sins forbidden in the sixth commandment?
before.answer: The sins forbidden in the sixth commandment are, all taking away the life of ourselves, or of others, except in case of public justice, lawful war, or necessary defense; the neglecting or withdrawing the lawful and necessary means of preservation of life; sinful anger, hatred, envy, desire of revenge; all excessive passions, distracting cares; immoderate use of meat, drink, labor, and recreations; provoking words, oppression, quarreling, striking, wounding, and: Whatsoever else tends to the destruction of the life of any.
before.right: Taking life except public justice, war, or defense; sinful anger, hatred, envy, revenge; immoderate use; provoking words; oppression; quarreling; striking

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Exodus 20:15 gives the words "You shall not steal," which is the eighth of the ten commandments in the order of Exodus 20:2-17.

before.question: Which is the eighth commandment?
before.answer: The eighth commandment is, You shall not steal.
before.right: The eighth commandment is, You shall not steal.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Luke 12:47-48 ties greater guilt to knowledge and entrusted position; Hebrews 10:29 to sins against Christ and the Spirit; 1 Corinthians 8:12 to wounding brethren; Numbers 15:30 to defiant sin; 2 Samuel 16:22 to sin done before all Israel.

before.question: What are those aggravations that make some sins more heinous than others?
before.answer: Sins receive their aggravations, 1. From the persons offending: if they be of riper age, greater experience or grace, eminent for profession, gifts, place, office, guides to others, and whose example is likely to be followed by others. 2. From the parties offended: if immediately against God, his attributes, and worship; against Christ, and his grace; the Holy Spirit, his witness, and workings; against superiors, men of eminency, and such as we stand especially related and engaged unto; against any of the saints, particularly weak brethren, the souls of them, or any other, and the common good of all or many. 3. From the nature and quality of the offense: if it be against the express letter of the law, break many commandments, contain in it many sins: if not only conceived in the heart, but breaks forth in words and actions, scandalize others, and admit of no reparation: if against means, mercies, judgments, light of nature, conviction of conscience, public or private admonition, censures of the church, civil punishments; and our prayers, purposes, promises, vows, covenants, and engagements to God or men: if done deliberately, wilfully, presumptuously, impudently, boastingly, maliciously, frequently, obstinately, with delight, continuance, or relapsing after repentance. 4. From circumstances of time and place: if on the Lord's day, or other times of divine worship; or immediately before or after these, or other helps to prevent or remedy such miscarriages: if in public, or in the presence of others, who are thereby likely to be provoked or defiled.
before.right: From the persons offending, parties offended, nature of offense, and circumstances of time and place

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Deuteronomy 6 has parents teach God's words to their children at home, and Isaiah 34:16 says "Search and read the scroll of the LORD." 1 Corinthians 14:16 implies Scripture must be understood by hearers, supporting translation into the people's language.

before.question: Is the word of God to be read by all?
before.answer: Although all are not to be permitted to read the word publicly to the congregation, yet all sorts of people are bound to read it apart by themselves, and with their families: to which end, the holy scriptures are to be translated out of the original into vulgar languages.
before.right: Not all permitted to read publicly; all bound to read privately with families; scriptures translated to vulgar languages

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: No one verse gives the whole answer, but together these show reverence for God's word, prayer for understanding, eager seeking, meditation, and obedience to what it says.

before.question: How is the word of God to be read?
before.answer: The holy scriptures are to be read with an high and reverent esteem of them; with a firm persuasion that they are the very word of God, and that he only can enable us to understand them; with desire to know, believe, and obey the will of God revealed in them; with diligence, and attention to the matter and scope of them; with meditation, application, self-denial, and prayer.
before.right: With reverent esteem, firm persuasion they are God's word, desire to obey, diligence, attention, meditation, application, self-denial, and prayer

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Hebrews 5:4 says no one takes the honor himself but must be called by God. 1 Timothy 3:2 requires an overseer to be able to teach, and 3:10 requires testing before serving. Together these teach gifting, testing, and call.

before.question: By whom is the word of God to be preached?
before.answer: The word of God is to be preached only by such as are sufficiently gifted, and also duly approved and called to that office.
before.right: Only by those sufficiently gifted, duly approved, and called to the office of preaching

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Taken together, these verses show the marks: sound doctrine (Titus 2:1), preaching in season and out of season (2 Tim 4:2), plain demonstration of the Spirit's power (1 Cor 2:4), the whole counsel of God (Acts 20:27), adapting to hearers (1 Cor 9:22), love (2 Cor 5:14), sincerity (2 Cor 2:17), and aim at salvation (1 Tim 4:16).

before.question: How is the word of God to be preached by those that are called thereunto?
before.answer: They that are called to labor in the ministry of the word, are to preach sound doctrine, diligently, in season and out of season; plainly, not in the enticing words of man's wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit, and of power; faithfully, making known the whole counsel of God; wisely, applying themselves to the necessities and capacities of the hearers; zealously, with fervent love to God and the souls of his people; sincerely, aiming at his glory, and their conversion, edification, and salvation.
before.right: Sound doctrine, plainly, faithfully the whole counsel, wisely, zealously, sincerely, with Spirit's demonstration

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Col 1:16 says all things, including thrones and dominions, were created; Heb 1:14 calls angels spirits; Ps 103:20-21 gives their strength, obedience and praise; Luke 20:36 says they cannot die; Luke 9:26 calls them holy; 2 Pet 2:4 shows they could sin and change.

before.question: How did God create angels?
before.answer: God created all the angels spirits, immortal, holy, excelling in knowledge, mighty in power, to execute his commandments, and to praise his name, yet subject to change.
before.right: God created angels immortal, holy spirits of knowledge and power, to execute commandments and praise God, yet subject to change.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: The word "sacrament" never appears, but the answer is drawn from the proofs: circumcision is a covenant sign, Christ instituted the Supper, Abraham's circumcision is a seal, and the cup and bread are participation in Christ.

before.question: What is a sacrament?
before.answer: A sacrament is a holy ordinance instituted by Christ in his church, to signify, seal, and exhibit unto those that are within the covenant of grace, the benefits of his mediation; to strengthen and increase their faith, and all other graces; to oblige them to obedience; to testify and cherish their love and communion one with another; and to distinguish them from those that are without.
before.right: Holy ordinance instituted by Christ to signify, seal, and exhibit benefits of his mediation to those in covenant of grace

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Baptism is set out as an outward sign, water, joined to an inward reality, the Spirit (Matt 3:11) or a clear conscience toward God (1 Pet 3:21). Romans 2:28-29 gives the outward/inward contrast behind this.

before.question: What are the parts of a sacrament?
before.answer: The parts of a sacrament are two; the one an outward and sensible sign, used according to Christ's own appointment; the other an inward and spiritual grace thereby signified.
before.right: Two parts: an outward sensible sign according to Christ's appointment, and an inward spiritual grace signified thereby

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Believers are to remember their baptism into Christ's death and resurrection, count themselves dead to sin and alive to God, live in holiness, and love one another as one body.

before.question: How is our Baptism to be improved by us?
before.answer: The needful but much neglected duty of improving our Baptism, is to be performed by us all our life long, especially in the time of temptation, and when we are present at the administration of it to others; by serious and thankful consideration of the nature of it, and of the ends for which Christ instituted it, the privileges and benefits conferred and sealed thereby, and our solemn vow made therein; by being humbled for our sinful defilement, our falling short of, and walking contrary to, the grace of baptism, and our engagements; by growing up to assurance of pardon of sin, and of all other blessings sealed to us in that sacrament; by drawing strength from the death and resurrection of Christ, into whom we are baptized, for the mortifying of sin, and quickening of grace; and by endeavoring to live by faith, to have our conversation in holiness and righteousness, as those that have therein given up their names to Christ; and to walk in brotherly love, as being baptized by the same Spirit into one body.
before.right: Serious thankful consideration of baptism's nature, benefits and vow; humbling for sin; assurance of pardon; strength from Christ's death

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Jesus blesses and breaks the bread, gives it to the disciples to eat, and gives the cup to drink, "in remembrance" of Him, with His body given and blood poured out for them.

before.question: How hath Christ appointed bread and wine to be given and received in the sacrament of the Lord's supper?
before.answer: Christ hath appointed the ministers of his word, in the administration of this sacrament of the Lord's Supper, to set apart the bread and wine from common use, by the word of institution, thanksgiving, and prayer; to take and break the bread, and to give both the bread and the wine to the communicants: who are, by the same appointment, to take and eat the bread, and to drink the wine, in thankful remembrance that the body of Christ was broken and given, and his blood shed, for them.
before.right: Ministers set apart bread and wine by word of institution, thanksgiving, and prayer; give to communicants who eat and drink

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Acts 3:21 says heaven must receive Christ, so His body is not corporally in the bread; 1 Corinthians 10:16 calls the cup and bread a participation in His blood and body, which the answer's spiritual feeding by faith draws out.

before.question: How do they that worthily communicate in the Lord's supper feed upon the body and blood of Christ therein?
before.answer: As the body and blood of Christ are not corporally or carnally present in, with, or under the bread and wine in the Lord's supper, and yet are spiritually present to the faith of the receiver, no less truly and really than the elements themselves are to their outward senses; so they that worthily communicate in the sacrament of the Lord's supper, do therein feed upon the body and blood of Christ, not after a corporal and carnal, but in a spiritual manner; yet truly and really, while by faith they receive and apply unto themselves Christ crucified, and all the benefits of his death.
before.right: Spiritually, not carnally, present to faith; truly and really receiving Christ crucified and his benefits

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Paul commands that each one examine himself before eating the bread and drinking the cup, and 2 Corinthians 13:5 tells believers to test themselves whether they are in the faith. The listed graces follow from these proof texts.

before.question: How are they that receive the sacrament of the Lord's supper to prepare themselves before they come unto it?
before.answer: They that receive the sacrament of the Lord's supper are, before they come, to prepare themselves thereunto, by examining themselves of their being in Christ, of their sins and wants; of the truth and measure of their knowledge, faith, repentance; love to God and the brethren, charity to all men, forgiving those that have done them wrong; of their desires after Christ, and of their new obedience; and by renewing the exercise of these graces, by serious meditation, and fervent prayer.
before.right: Examine their being in Christ, faith, sins, love to God and brethren, forgiveness; renew by prayer

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Paul desires to be found in Christ (Phil 3:9) and the Lord's name calls for turning from iniquity (2 Tim 2:19). The believing father confesses unbelief and asks for help (Mark 9:24), and the bruised reed is not broken (Matt 12:20).

before.question: May one who doubteth of his being in Christ, or of his due preparation, come to the Lord's supper?
before.answer: One who doubteth of his being in Christ, or of his due preparation to the sacrament of the Lord's supper, may have true interest in Christ, though he be not yet assured thereof; and in God's account hath it, if he be duly affected with the apprehension of the want of it, and unfeignedly desires to be found in Christ, and to depart from iniquity: in which case (because promises are made, and this sacrament is appointed, for the relief even of weak and doubting Christians) he is to bewail his unbelief, and labor to have his doubts resolved; and, so doing, he may and ought to come to the Lord's supper, that he may be further strengthened.
before.right: He may have true interest in Christ if he sincerely desires Christ, and he should come to the Lord's supper to be strengthened

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Paul tells the church not to associate with or even eat with a professing brother who is sexually immoral or otherwise scandalous, and warns that unworthy eating brings judgment, so each must examine himself first.

before.question: May any who profess the faith, and desire to come to the Lord's supper, be kept from it?
before.answer: Such as are found to be ignorant or scandalous, notwithstanding their profession of the faith, and desire to come to the Lord's supper, may and ought to be kept from that sacrament, by the power which Christ hath left in his church, until they receive instruction, and manifest their reformation.
before.right: Yes; the ignorant and scandalous are to be excluded by church power until reformed

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Communicants are to examine themselves and discern the Lord's body, proclaiming his death, and to do this in remembrance of Christ. The answer's wider duties are drawn from these proof texts.

before.question: What is required of them that receive the sacrament of the Lord's supper in the time of the administration of it?
before.answer: It is required of them that receive the sacrament of the Lord's supper, that, during the time of the administration of it, with all holy reverence and attention they wait upon God in that ordinance, diligently observe the sacramental elements and actions, heedfully discern the Lord's body, and affectionately meditate on his death and sufferings, and thereby stir up themselves to a vigorous exercise of their graces; in judging themselves, and sorrowing for sin; in earnest hungering and thirsting after Christ, feeding on him by faith, receiving of his fulness, trusting in his merits, rejoicing in his love, giving thanks for his grace; in renewing of their covenant with God, and love to all the saints.
before.right: With reverence and attention, discern the Lord's body, meditate on death, judge themselves, feed by faith

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Scripture teaches self-examination (1 Cor 11:31), thanks to God for help and comfort (Ps 28:7), fulfilling vows (Ps 50:14), godly sorrow after failing (2 Cor 7:11), and continued devotion to the breaking of bread (Acts 2:42).

before.question: What is the duty of Christians, after they have received the sacrament of the Lord's supper?
before.answer: The duty of Christians, after they have received the sacrament of the Lord's supper, is seriously to consider how they have behaved themselves therein, and with what success; if they find quickening and comfort, to bless God for it, beg the continuance of it, watch against relapses, fulfil their vows, and encourage themselves to a frequent attendance on that ordinance: but if they find no present benefit, more exactly to review their preparation to, and carriage at, the sacrament; in both which, if they can approve themselves to God and their own consciences, they are to wait for the fruit of it in due time: but, if they see they have failed in either, they are to be humbled, and to attend upon it afterwards with more care and diligence.
before.right: Reflect on their behavior; if blessed, bless God and attend frequently; if not, review and improve

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: The Lord instituted both baptism and the Lord's supper, both convey Christ and his benefits, both are seals of the covenant, are given by called stewards, and last until he comes.

before.question: Wherein do the sacraments of baptism and the Lord's supper agree?
before.answer: The sacraments of baptism and the Lord's supper agree, in that the author of both is God; the spiritual part of both is Christ and his benefits; both are seals of the same covenant, are to be dispensed by ministers of the gospel, and by none other; and to be continued in the church of Christ until his second coming.
before.right: Both authored by God; spiritual part is Christ and his benefits; seals of same covenant; dispensed by gospel ministers only

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Baptism is the washing of new birth and being clothed with Christ, promised to children too, and Ephesians speaks of one baptism; the Supper is bread and wine, shared often, after self-examination.

before.question: Wherein do the sacraments of baptism and the Lord's supper differ?
before.answer: The sacraments of baptism and the Lord's supper differ, in that baptism is to be administered but once, with water, to be a sign and seal of our regeneration and ingrafting into Christ, and that even to infants; whereas the Lord's supper is to be administered often, in the elements of bread and wine, to represent and exhibit Christ as spiritual nourishment to the soul, and to confirm our continuance and growth in him, and that only to such as are of years and ability to examine themselves.
before.right: Baptism administered once with water for regeneration; Lord's supper administered often with bread and wine for spiritual nourishment

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Worship belongs to the Lord God alone (Matt 4:10); only God knows hearts, pardons iniquity, hears prayer, and fulfills desires (1 Kgs 8:39; Mic 7:18; Ps 65:2; Ps 145:19); so people are to call upon Him (Ps 50:15).

before.question: Are we to pray unto God only?
before.answer: God only being able to search the hearts, hear the requests, pardon the sins, and fulfil the desires of all; and only to be believed in, and worshiped with religious worship; prayer, which is a special part thereof, is to be made by all to him alone, and to none other.
before.right: God only can search hearts, hear requests, and pardon sins; prayer is to be made to him alone

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Praying in Christ's name means asking on his authority and for his sake, as Daniel asks "for Your sake," and approaching with confidence through the great high priest. Saying his name alone does not suffice.

before.question: What is it to pray in the name of Christ?
before.answer: To pray in the name of Christ is, in obedience to his command, and in confidence on his promises, to ask mercy for his sake; not by bare mentioning of his name, but by drawing our encouragement to pray, and our boldness, strength, and hope of acceptance in prayer, from Christ and his mediation.
before.right: In confidence on his promises, ask mercy for his sake, drawing boldness from Christ's mediation

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Sin separates people from God (Isa 59:2), and Christ is the only way to the Father and the one mediator (John 14:6; 1 Tim 2:5), fit to save and intercede (Heb 7:25-26).

before.question: Why are we to pray in the name of Christ?
before.answer: The sinfulness of man, and his distance from God by reason thereof, being so great, as that we can have no access into his presence without a mediator; and there being none in heaven or earth appointed to, or fit for, that glorious work but Christ alone, we are to pray in no other name but his only.
before.right: Man's sinfulness and distance from God make Christ alone the appointed mediator; we must pray in his name

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Romans 8:26-27 says we do not know how to pray, so the Spirit helps our weakness and intercedes for us, and God searches hearts and knows that mind. Zechariah 12:10 says God pours out a spirit of prayer.

before.question: How doth the Spirit help us to pray?
before.answer: We not knowing: What to pray for as we ought, the Spirit helps our infirmities, by enabling us to understand both for whom, and: What, and: How prayer is to be made; and by working and quickening in our hearts (although not in all persons, nor at all times, in the same measure) those apprehensions, affections, and graces which are requisite for the right performance of that duty.
before.right: Spirit helps by enabling understanding of for whom, what, and how to pray; works requisite graces in our hearts

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Scripture teaches prayer for everyone, kings and those in authority, the saints, Paul and ministers, enemies, future believers, and one another, and not for a sin unto death; David's prayer ends at the child's death.

before.question: For whom are we to pray?
before.answer: We are to pray for the whole church of Christ upon earth; for magistrates, and ministers; for ourselves, our brethren, yea, our enemies; and for all sorts of men living, or that shall live hereafter; but not for the dead, nor for those that are known to have sinned the sin unto death.
before.right: Whole church, magistrates, ministers, ourselves, brethren, enemies, and all men living or to come; but not the dead

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Jesus teaches us to pray that God's name be hallowed and His kingdom come, Psalm 122:6 bids prayer for Jerusalem's peace, Matthew 7:11 promises good things to those who ask, and 1 John 5:14 limits asking to what is according to His will.

before.question: For what things are we to pray?
before.answer: We are to pray for all things tending to the glory of God, the welfare of the church, our own or others good; but not for anything that is unlawful.
before.right: All things tending to God's glory, the church's welfare, our own or others' good; but not unlawful things

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: The answer summarizes the manner of prayer taught across these passages: reverence before God's majesty, humility over sin, a penitent and thankful heart, sincere faith, perseverance, and submission to God's will.

before.question: How are we to pray?
before.answer: We are to pray with an awful apprehension of the majesty of God, and deep sense of our own unworthiness, necessities, and sins; with penitent, thankful, and enlarged hearts; with understanding, faith, sincerity, fervency, love, and perseverance, waiting upon him, with humble submission to his will.
before.right: With apprehension of God's majesty, sense of unworthiness, penitent and thankful hearts, understanding, faith, sincerity, fervency, love, and perseverance

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Jesus gives the Lord's prayer as words to be said ("this is how you should pray," "When you pray, say"), so it may be used as a prayer. The verses do not mention understanding, faith, or reverence, which the answer adds.

before.question: How is the Lord's prayer to be used?
before.answer: The Lord's prayer is not only for direction, as a pattern, according to which we are to make other prayers; but may also be used as a prayer, so that it be done with understanding, faith, reverence, and other graces necessary to the right performance of the duty of prayer.
before.right: As pattern for other prayers and as prayer itself, with understanding, faith, reverence, and other necessary graces

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Matthew 6:9-13 shows an opening address ("Our Father in heaven") and the petitions. The three-part division into preface, petitions, and conclusion is the catechism's own structure, not stated in the verses.
creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.doubt: The shown verses contain a preface and petitions but no concluding part, since the BSB text ends at "deliver us from the evil one" without the traditional doxology.

before.question: Of how many parts doth the Lord's prayer consist?
before.answer: The Lord's prayer consists of three parts; a preface, petitions, and a conclusion.
before.right: Three parts: a preface, petitions, and a conclusion

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Jude 1:6 and 2 Peter 2:4 show angels who sinned kept in chains for judgment, Job 1:12 shows God limiting Satan, and Hebrews 1:14 shows angels sent to serve. Ordering all their sins to God's glory is inference.

before.question: What is God's providence towards the angels?
before.answer: God by his providence permitted some of the angels, wilfully and irrecoverably, to fall into sin and damnation, limiting and ordering that, and all their sins, to his own glory; and established the rest in holiness and happiness; employing them all, at his pleasure, in the administrations of his power, mercy, and justice.
before.right: God permitted some angels to fall willfully into sin and damnation; He established the rest in holiness and employs both to His glory.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Psalm 51:5 says David was sinful from conception, and John 3:6 says flesh is born of flesh, so sin passes through natural birth from parents.

before.question: How is original sin conveyed from our first parents unto their posterity?
before.answer: Original sin is conveyed from our first parents unto their posterity by natural generation, so as all that proceed from them in that way are conceived and born in sin.
before.right: Original sin passes from our first parents through natural generation to all their descendants conceived and born in sin.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Inward punishments appear as darkened understanding and hardened hearts (Eph 4:18), a depraved mind and vile passions (Rom 1:26, 28), strong delusion (2 Thess 2:11), and terror of conscience (Isa 33:14). Outward ones are the cursed ground (Gen 3:17), bodily and family curses (Deut 28:15-18), and death (Rom 6:23).

before.question: What are the punishments of sin in this world?
before.answer: The punishments of sin in this world are either inward, as blindness of mind, a reprobate sense, strong delusions, hardness of heart, horror of conscience, and vile affections; or outward, as the curse of God upon the creatures for our sakes, and all other evils that befall us in our bodies, names, estates, relations, and employments; together with death itself.
before.right: Inward: blindness of mind, hardness of heart; outward: God's curse on creation, bodily evils, and death.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: 2 Thessalonians 1:9 gives eternal destruction and separation from the Lord's presence; Mark 9:48 and Revelation 20:10 give fire that is never quenched and torment day and night forever.

before.question: What are the punishments of sin in the world to come?
before.answer: The punishments of sin in the world to come are everlasting separation from the comfortable presence of God, and most grievous torments in soul and body, without intermission, in hell fire forever.
before.right: Everlasting separation from God's comfortable presence and most grievous torments in soul and body, without intermission, in hell fire forever.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Galatians 3:16 identifies the promised "seed" as Christ, and Romans 5:18-19 presents Christ as the one man whose obedience makes "the many" righteous, as Adam's sin made many sinners.

before.question: With whom was the covenant of grace made?
before.answer: The covenant of grace was made with Christ as the second Adam, and in him with all the elect as his seed.
before.right: The covenant of grace was made with Christ as the second Adam, and in him with all the elect as his seed.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: God gives His Son so that whoever believes has eternal life (John 3:16), Christ is the mediator of the new covenant (Heb 9:15), God puts His Spirit within His people to cause obedience (Ezek 36:27), and faith is God's gift (Eph 2:8).

before.question: How is the grace of God manifested in the second covenant?
before.answer: The grace of God is manifested in the second covenant, in that he freely provideth and offereth to sinners a Mediator, and life and salvation by him; and requiring faith as the condition to interest them in him, promiseth and giveth his Holy Spirit to all his elect, to work in them that faith, with all other saving graces; and to enable them unto all holy obedience, as the evidence of the truth of their faith and thankfulness to God, and as the way which he hath appointed them to salvation.
before.right: God freely provides a Mediator and life and salvation by Him; He gives His Holy Spirit to work faith in believers and enable holy obedience.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Paul contrasts the new covenant ministry of the Spirit with the earlier ministry of Moses, engraved on stone, calling it a ministry of death and condemnation. The administrations differ, though the verses never name "covenant of grace" outright.

before.question: Was the covenant of grace always administered after one and the same manner?
before.answer: The covenant of grace was not always administered after the same manner, but the administrations of it under the Old Testament were different from those under the New.
before.right: The covenant of grace was not always administered the same way; Old Testament administrations differed from New Testament administrations.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: The law's sacrifices and ordinances are a shadow of the coming good things, circumcision is a seal of faith, Christ is the Passover lamb, prophets proclaimed these days, and redemption from Old Covenant transgressions came through Christ's death.

before.question: How was the covenant of grace administered under the Old Testament?
before.answer: The covenant of grace was administered under the Old Testament, by promises, prophecies, sacrifices, circumcision, the passover, and other types and ordinances, which did all foresignify Christ then to come, and were for that time sufficient to build up the elect in faith in the promised Messiah, by whom they then had full remission of sin, and eternal salvation.
before.right: By promises, prophecies, sacrifices, circumcision, the passover and types pointing to Christ, sufficient for full remission and salvation.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Christ commands the gospel be preached to every creature and disciples be made of all nations by baptizing, and the Lord's Supper is instituted as the new covenant in His blood; 2 Corinthians 3 and Hebrews 8 describe this ministry as better and more glorious.

before.question: How is the covenant of grace administered under the New Testament?
before.answer: Under the New Testament, when Christ the substance was exhibited, the same covenant of grace was and still is to be administered in the preaching of the word, and the administration of the sacraments of Baptism and the Lord's Supper; in which grace and salvation are held forth in more fulness, evidence, and efficacy, to all nations.
before.right: By preaching the Word and administering Baptism and Lord's Supper; grace and salvation are held forth in fuller evidence and efficacy to all nations.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: 1 Timothy 2:5 names the one mediator as the man Christ Jesus, and Hebrews 9:15 calls Christ the mediator of the new covenant. John 1:14 and Colossians 2:9 show the Son as God becoming flesh, with the fullness of Deity dwelling in bodily form.

before.question: Who is the Mediator of the covenant of grace?
before.answer: The only Mediator of the covenant of grace is the Lord Jesus Christ, who, being the eternal Son of God, of one substance and equal with the Father, in the fulness of time became man, and so was and continues to be God and man, in two entire distinct natures, and one person, forever.
before.right: The Lord Jesus Christ, eternal Son of God, equal with the Father, is the sole Mediator of the covenant of grace.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Scripture shows the Mediator's divine worth: his eternal Spirit gives his sacrifice worth (Heb 9:14), he is "our great God and Savior" (Titus 2:13), and death could not hold him (Acts 2:24).

before.question: Why was it requisite that the Mediator should be God?
before.answer: It was requisite that the Mediator should be God, that he might sustain and keep the human nature from sinking under the infinite wrath of God, and the power of death; give worth and efficacy to his sufferings, obedience, and intercession; and to satisfy God's justice, procure his favor, purchase a peculiar people, give his Spirit to them, conquer all their enemies, and bring them to everlasting salvation.
before.right: God's Mediator must be God to sustain human nature under wrath, give worth to His sacrifice, satisfy justice, and bring salvation.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Christ was born of a woman and under the law to redeem those under the law, sharing our flesh and blood, made like His brothers to be a merciful high priest, and tempted as we are yet without sin, so we may approach boldly.

before.question: Why was it requisite that the Mediator should be man?
before.answer: It was requisite that the Mediator should be man, that he might advance our nature, perform obedience to the law, suffer and make intercession for us in our nature, have a fellow feeling of our infirmities; that we might receive the adoption of sons, and have comfort and access with boldness unto the throne of grace.
before.right: The Mediator must be man to obey the law, suffer and intercede for us, and give us access to God's grace.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Hebrews 9:14 shows one person, Christ, offering himself through the eternal Spirit to cleanse our consciences; Matthew 1:23 names that one person "God with us." The answer follows from these.

before.question: Why was it requisite that the Mediator should be God and man in one person?
before.answer: It was requisite that the Mediator, who was to reconcile God and man, should himself be both God and man, and this in one person, that the proper works of each nature might be accepted of God for us, and relied on by us, as the works of the whole person.
before.right: So the works of His divine and human natures are accepted by God for us.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Matthew 1:21 states the name Jesus is given "because He will save His people from their sins," which matches the answer directly.

before.question: Why was our Mediator called Jesus?
before.answer: Our Mediator was called Jesus, because he saves his people from their sins.
before.right: Our Mediator was called Jesus, because he saves his people from their sins.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Philippians 2:6-8 has Christ emptying himself, taking the form of a servant, and dying on a cross; Luke 1:31 gives his conception and birth; Acts 2:24 shows God raising him from death.

before.question: What was the estate of Christ's humiliation?
before.answer: The estate of Christ's humiliation was that low condition, wherein he for our sakes, emptying himself of his glory, took upon him the form of a servant, in his conception and birth, life, death, and after his death, until his resurrection.
before.right: That low condition wherein Christ, emptying Himself of glory, took the form of a servant from conception through death until resurrection.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: The eternal Son at the Father's side becomes flesh (John 1:14, 1:18), is born of a woman (Gal 4:4), and is laid in a manger with no room in the inn (Luke 2:7).

before.question: How did Christ humble himself in his conception and birth?
before.answer: Christ humbled himself in his conception and birth, in that, being from all eternity the Son of God, at the Father's side, he was pleased in the fulness of time to become the son of man, made of a woman of low estate, and to be born of her; with divers circumstances of more than ordinary abasement.
before.right: From eternity the Son of God at the Father's side, He became son of man, made of a woman of low estate, born in abasement.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Christ was born under the law (Gal 4:4) and came to fulfill it (Matt 5:17), was tempted by the devil (Matt 4:1-11), endured hostility from sinners (Heb 12:3), and was tempted in every way we are (Heb 4:15).

before.question: How did Christ humble himself in his life?
before.answer: Christ humbled himself in his life, by subjecting himself to the law, which he perfectly fulfilled; and by conflicting with the indignities of the world, temptations of Satan, and infirmities in his flesh, whether common to the nature of man, or particularly accompanying that his low condition.
before.right: By subjecting Himself to the law and perfectly fulfilling it; by conflicting with the world's indignities, Satan's temptations, and infirmities.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: The verses show each part: Judas's betrayal, the disciples fleeing, Christ despised and rejected, Pilate's sentence and the mockery and beating, anguish in Gethsemane, forsaken by God, a guilt offering, death on a cross, and the curse of the cross.

before.question: How did Christ humble himself in his death?
before.answer: Christ humbled himself in his death, in that having been betrayed by Judas, forsaken by his disciples, scorned and rejected by the world, condemned by Pilate, and tormented by his persecutors; having also conflicted with the terrors of death, and the powers of darkness, felt and borne the weight of God's wrath, he laid down his life an offering for sin, enduring the painful, shameful, and cursed death of the cross.
before.right: Betrayed, forsaken, rejected, condemned, and tormented, he bore God's wrath and died the painful, shameful, cursed death of the cross.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Christ was buried and raised on the third day (1 Cor 15:4), and His soul was not abandoned to Hades nor His body to decay (Acts 2:31). Together these teach burial, continuing among the dead, until the third day.

before.question: Wherein consisted Christ's humiliation after his death?
before.answer: Christ's humiliation after his death consisted in his being buried, and continuing in the state of the dead, and under the power of death till the third day; which hath been otherwise expressed in these words, he descended into hell.
before.right: Christ was buried and remained under death's power for three days; expressed as 'He descended into hell.'

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Acts 2:27 says he did not see decay; Luke 24:39 shows a risen body of flesh and bones; Rom 1:4 and 4:25 show him declared Son of God and raised for justification; 1 Cor 15:20-22 shows him as firstfruits.

before.question: How was Christ exalted in his resurrection?
before.answer: Christ was exalted in his resurrection, in that, not having seen corruption in death (of which it was not possible for him to be held), and having the very same body in which he suffered, with the essential properties thereof (but without mortality, and other common infirmities belonging to this life), really united to his soul, he rose again from the dead the third day by his own power; whereby he declared himself to be the Son of God, to have satisfied divine justice, to have vanquished death, and him that had the power of it, and to be Lord of quick and dead: all which he did as a public person, the head of his church, for their justification, quickening in grace, support against enemies, and to assure them of their resurrection from the dead at the last day.
before.right: He rose in the same body, uncorrupted, declared Himself God's Son, and vanquished death as Head of His Church.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: The verses show the forty days of appearances and teaching about the kingdom, the visible ascent into heaven, the commission to preach to all nations, the forerunner entering heaven, the preparing of a place, and heaven receiving Christ until the restoration.

before.question: How was Christ exalted in his ascension?
before.answer: Christ was exalted in his ascension, in that having after his resurrection often appeared unto and conversed with his apostles, speaking to them of the things pertaining to the kingdom of God, and giving them commission to preach the gospel to all nations, forty days after his resurrection, he, in our nature, and as our head, triumphing over enemies, visibly went up into the highest heavens, there to receive gifts for men, to raise up our affections thither, and to prepare a place for us, where himself is, and shall continue till his second coming at the end of the world.
before.right: After forty days appearing and commissioning apostles to preach, He visibly ascended to highest heavens as our head, triumphing to prepare a place for us.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: God exalts Christ to the highest place (Phil 2:9), gives Him power over all things and headship for the church (Eph 1:22), makes enemies His footstool (Ps 110:1), gives ministers (Eph 4:11-12), intercedes (Rom 8:34), and fills Him with joy (Ps 16:11).

before.question: How is Christ exalted in his sitting at the right hand of God?
before.answer: Christ is exalted in his sitting at the right hand of God, in that as God-man he is advanced to the highest favor with God the Father, with all fulness of joy, glory, and power over all things in heaven and earth; and doth gather and defend his church, and subdue their enemies; furnisheth his ministers and people with gifts and graces, and maketh intercession for them.
before.right: Christ at God's right hand has full power and glory, defends His church, furnishes gifts and graces, and intercedes for us.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Christ entered heaven to appear before God on our behalf (Heb 9:24), interceding for us (Rom 8:34), as our advocate for sins (1 John 2:1-2), so we approach the throne of grace with confidence (Heb 4:16).

before.question: How doth Christ make intercession?
before.answer: Christ maketh intercession, by his appearing in our nature continually before the Father in heaven, in the merit of his obedience and sacrifice on earth, declaring his will to have it applied to all believers; answering all accusations against them, and procuring for them quiet of conscience, notwithstanding daily failings, access with boldness to the throne of grace, and acceptance of their persons and services.
before.right: By appearing in our nature before the Father, presenting his merit and sacrifice, and answering accusations against believers.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: The answer is drawn from the question's proof texts: Christ was rejected by men (Acts 3:14-15), returns in power and glory with angels (Matt 24:30; Luke 9:26; Matt 25:31), with a command, archangel's voice and trumpet (1 Thess 4:16), to judge in righteousness (Acts 17:31).

before.question: How is Christ to be exalted in his coming again to judge the world?
before.answer: Christ is to be exalted in his coming again to judge the world, in that he, who was unjustly judged and condemned by wicked men, shall come again at the last day in great power, and in the full manifestation of his own glory, and of his Father's, with all his holy angels, with a loud command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God, to judge the world in righteousness.
before.right: Christ shall come at the last day in great power and glory, with His holy angels, to judge the world in righteousness.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Hebrews 9:12 says Christ entered once for all by His own blood, thus securing eternal redemption. 2 Corinthians 1:20 says all God's promises are "Yes" in Christ, which supports the wider "all other benefits of the covenant."

before.question: What benefits has Christ procured by His mediation?
before.answer: Christ, by His mediation, has procured redemption, with all other benefits of the covenant of grace.
before.right: Christ, by His mediation, has procured redemption, with all other benefits of the covenant of grace.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Christ lays down His life for His sheep, and everyone the Father gives Him comes to Him; faith itself is the gift of God. The answer follows from these verses.

before.question: Who are made partakers of redemption through Christ?
before.answer: Redemption is certainly applied and effectually communicated to all those for whom Christ has purchased it; in time they are enabled by the Holy Spirit to believe in Christ according to the gospel.
before.right: Those for whom Christ purchased redemption, who are enabled by the Holy Spirit to believe the gospel.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Matthew 28:19 names the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; Acts 4:28 shows God's decided purpose being carried out; Hebrews 11:6 shows that God exists and rewards those who seek Him.

before.question: What do the scriptures make known of God?
before.answer: The scriptures make known what God is, the persons in the Godhead, his decrees, and the execution of his decrees.
before.right: The scriptures make known what God is, the persons in the Godhead, his decrees, and the execution of them.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Acts 4:12 says salvation is in no one else and no other name, and Romans 10:14 says people cannot believe in one they have not heard. Together they teach that unhearing people cannot be saved by light of nature.

before.question: Can they who have never heard the gospel, and so know not Jesus Christ, nor believe in him, be saved by their living according to the light of nature?
before.answer: They who, having never heard the gospel, know not Jesus Christ, and believe not in him, cannot be saved, be they never so diligent to frame their lives according to the light of nature, or the laws of that religion which they profess; neither is there salvation in any other, but in Christ alone, who is the Savior only of his body the church.
before.right: No; salvation is in Christ alone, however diligently they live by the light of nature or their own religion.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Romans 9:6 says not all descended from Israel are Israel, and Matthew 7:21 says not everyone who calls Jesus Lord will enter the kingdom. Together they teach that outward church membership does not guarantee salvation.

before.question: Are all they saved who hear the gospel, and live in the church?
before.answer: All that hear the gospel, and live in the visible church, are not saved; but they only who are true members of the church invisible.
before.right: Not all who hear the gospel and live in the visible church are saved, but only true members of the invisible church.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Scripture shows God covering and shielding Zion (Isa 4:5-6; Isa 31:5), the believers' fellowship and ministry (Acts 2:42; Eph 4:11-12), the gospel promising salvation to believers (Mark 16:16), and none who come to Christ turned away (John 6:37).

before.question: What are the special privileges of the visible church?
before.answer: The visible church has the privilege of being under God's special care and government; of being protected and preserved in all ages, notwithstanding the opposition of all enemies; and of enjoying the communion of saints, the ordinary means of salvation, and offers of grace by Christ to all its members in the ministry of the gospel, testifying that whoever believes in Him will be saved, and excluding none who come to Him.
before.right: God's special care and protection, communion of saints, means of salvation, and gospel offers excluding none who come.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: John 11:52 speaks of God's scattered children gathered together into one, and Ephesians 1:22-23 names Christ as head over the church, which is His body. Together they teach the answer's content.

before.question: What is the invisible church?
before.answer: The invisible church is the whole number of the elect, that have been, are, or shall be gathered into one under Christ the head.
before.right: The invisible church is the whole number of the elect, that have been, are, or shall be gathered into one under Christ the head.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Believers are made alive, raised, and seated with Christ by grace (Eph 2:5-6), and Christ wills that they be with Him and see His glory (John 17:24). Union, communion, grace, and glory are taught together.

before.question: What special benefits do the members of the invisible church enjoy by Christ?
before.answer: The members of the invisible church by Christ enjoy union and communion with him in grace and glory.
before.right: Union and communion with him in grace and glory.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Believers are one with the Lord in spirit, Christ is head of the church as husband is of wife, none can snatch them from His hand, they are called into fellowship with His Son, and salvation is by grace as God's gift.

before.question: What is that union which the elect have with Christ?
before.answer: The union which the elect have with Christ is the work of God's grace, whereby they are spiritually and mystically, yet really and inseparably, joined to Christ as their head and husband; which is done in their effectual calling.
before.right: God's grace whereby the elect are joined to Christ as head and husband in their effectual calling

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Acts 13:48 says those appointed to eternal life believe, Matthew 22:14 says many are called but few chosen, and Matthew 13:20-21 and Hebrews 6:4-6 describe those who receive the word but fall away. Psalm 81:11-12 shows God giving over those who refuse to listen.

before.question: Are the elect only effectually called?
before.answer: All the elect, and they only, are effectually called; although others may be, and often are, outwardly called by the ministry of the word, and have some common operations of the Spirit; who, for their wilful neglect and contempt of the grace offered to them, being justly left in their unbelief, do never truly come to Jesus Christ.
before.right: All the elect, and only they, are effectually called; others may be outwardly called but never truly come to Christ

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Believers are "in Christ Jesus," and He is their righteousness (justification), holiness (sanctification), and redemption; Ephesians 1:5 adds adoption through Jesus Christ.

before.question: What is the communion in grace which the members of the invisible church have with Christ?
before.answer: The communion in grace which the members of the invisible church have with Christ, is their partaking of the virtue of his mediation, in their justification, adoption, sanctification, and whatever else, in this life, manifests their union with him.
before.right: Partaking of the virtue of Christ's mediation in justification, adoption, sanctification, and whatever manifests union with him

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Romans 3:24 says we are justified freely by God's grace through Christ's redemption; Romans 8:32 shows God giving His Son; 2 Corinthians 5:21 shows imputed righteousness; Ephesians 2:8 says faith is God's gift.

before.question: How is justification an act of God's free grace?
before.answer: Although Christ, by his obedience and death, did make a proper, real, and full satisfaction to God's justice in the behalf of them that are justified; yet inasmuch as God accepteth the satisfaction from a surety, which he might have demanded of them, and did provide this surety, his own only Son, imputing his righteousness to them, and requiring nothing of them for their justification but faith, which also is his gift, their justification is to them of free grace.
before.right: Christ made full satisfaction for the justified; God accepts it from a surety and imputes Christ's righteousness, requiring only faith

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: No single verse gives the full definition, but together they teach it: hearing and believing the gospel by the Spirit (Eph 1:13), receiving Christ for forgiveness and righteousness (John 1:12, Phil 3:9, Acts 10:43), convicted of sin (Acts 2:37), and dead in sins (Eph 2:1).

before.question: What is justifying faith?
before.answer: Justifying faith is a saving grace, wrought in the heart of a sinner by the Spirit and word of God, whereby he, being convinced of his sin and misery, and of the disability in himself and all other creatures to recover him out of his lost condition, not only assenteth to the truth of the promise of the gospel, but receiveth and resteth upon Christ and his righteousness, therein held forth, for pardon of sin, and for the accepting and accounting of his person righteous in the sight of God for salvation.
before.right: Saving grace wrought by Spirit and word; conviction of sin and misery; receiving and resting on Christ and his righteousness for pardon

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Paul rejects a righteousness from the law and receives the righteousness that comes through faith in Christ, justified by faith apart from works. The word "instrument" is the catechism's own summary of this.
creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.doubt: Romans 4:5 says faith itself "is credited as righteousness," which sits uneasily with the answer's denial that the act of faith is credited, so the answer reads "faith" there as the means of receiving Christ.

before.question: How does faith justify a sinner in the sight of God?
before.answer: Faith justifies a sinner in the sight of God, not because of the other graces that always accompany it, or because of good works that are its fruits, nor because the grace of faith or any act of it is credited to him for his justification; but only because it is the instrument by which he receives and applies Christ and His righteousness.
before.right: Faith justifies not as good works or faith itself imputed, but as instrument to receive and apply Christ's righteousness

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Romans 4:6-8 says God credits righteousness apart from works and does not count sin, while Ezekiel 36:27 has God's Spirit enabling obedience. Philippians 3:12-14 and 1 John 1:8 show believers not yet perfect here.

before.question: Wherein do justification and sanctification differ?
before.answer: Although sanctification be inseparably joined with justification, yet they differ, in that God in justification imputeth the righteousness of Christ; in sanctification his Spirit infuseth grace, and enableth to the exercise thereof; in the former, sin is pardoned; in the other, it is subdued: the one doth equally free all believers from the revenging wrath of God, and that perfectly in this life, that they never fall into condemnation; the other is neither equal in all, nor in this life perfect in any, but growing up to perfection.
before.right: Justification imputes Christ's righteousness, pardons sin, perfectly frees from wrath; sanctification infuses grace, subdues sin, grows but never perfect

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Paul says nothing good lives in his flesh and that another law wars in his body against the law of his mind, so sin remaining in the believer is the source of the imperfection.

before.question: Whence ariseth the imperfection of sanctification in believers?
before.answer: The imperfection of sanctification in believers ariseth from the remnants of sin abiding in every part of them, and the perpetual lustings of the flesh against the spirit; whereby they are often foiled with temptations, and fall into many sins, are hindered in all their spiritual services, and their best works are imperfect and defiled in the sight of God.
before.right: Remnants of sin and flesh's lusts against spirit cause temptations, sins, hindered services, and imperfect works before God

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Christ's sheep "will never perish" and no one can snatch them from His hand; God promises never to turn away from doing good to them, and believers are shielded by God's power through faith.

before.question: Can true believers, despite their imperfections, temptations and sins, totally or finally fall away from the state of grace?
before.answer: No. True believers, by reason of the unchangeable love of God, and his decree and covenant to give them perseverance, their inseparable union with Christ, his continual intercession for them, and the Spirit and seed of God abiding in them, can neither totally nor finally fall away from the state of grace, but are kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation.
before.right: No, they are kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Deuteronomy 6:4 says the LORD is One, and Jeremiah 10:10 calls the LORD the true God and the living God, so the answer that there is one only, living and true God is stated.

before.question: Are there more Gods than one?
before.answer: There is but one only, the living and true God.
before.right: There is but one only, the living and true God.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: John wrote so that believers may know they have eternal life (1 John 5:13). The Spirit bears witness with our spirit that we are God's children (Romans 8:16), and Hebrews 6:11 urges diligence to make hope sure.

before.question: Can true believers be infallibly assured that they are in the estate of grace, and that they shall persevere therein unto salvation?
before.answer: Such as truly believe in Christ, and endeavor to walk in all good conscience before him, may, without extraordinary revelation, by faith grounded upon the truth of God's promises, and by the Spirit enabling them to discern in themselves those graces to which the promises of life are made, and bearing witness with their spirits that they are the children of God, be infallibly assured that they are in the estate of grace, and shall persevere therein unto salvation.
before.right: True believers may be infallibly assured by faith grounded in God's promises and the Spirit's witness with their spirits.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Psalm 88 shows a believer in despair and God seemingly rejecting him, and Isaiah 54 says God forsook His people for a moment, yet His loving devotion will not depart. Psalm 73:23 adds that God is always with them.

before.question: Are all true believers at all times assured of their present being in the estate of grace, and that they shall be saved?
before.answer: Assurance of grace and salvation not being of the essence of faith, true believers may wait long before they obtain it; and, after the enjoyment thereof, may have it weakened and intermitted, through manifold distempers, sins, temptations, and desertions; yet are they never left without such a presence and support of the Spirit of God as keeps them from sinking into utter despair.
before.right: True believers may lack assurance long or lose it through temptations, but the Spirit prevents them from sinking into despair.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Believers are being transformed into Christ's image now (2 Cor 3:18), will be with Him in Paradise the day they die (Luke 23:43), and will always be with the Lord at His coming (1 Thess 4:17).

before.question: What is the communion in glory which the members of the invisible church have with Christ?
before.answer: The communion in glory which the members of the invisible church have with Christ, is in this life, immediately after death, and at last perfected at the resurrection and day of judgment.
before.right: Communion in glory in this life, immediately after death, and perfected at resurrection and day of judgment

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Believers are raised and seated with Christ (Eph 2:6), given the Spirit as a pledge (2 Cor 1:22), with God's love poured out and peace, joy in the Spirit, and hope of glory (Rom 5:1-5; 14:17). The wicked face wrath and fearful expectation of judgment (Rom 2:8; Heb 10:27).

before.question: What is the communion in glory with Christ which the members of the invisible church enjoy in this life?
before.answer: The members of the invisible church have communicated to them in this life the firstfruits of glory with Christ, as they are members of him their head, and so in him are interested in that glory which he is fully possessed of; and, as an earnest thereof, enjoy the sense of God's love, peace of conscience, joy in the Holy Spirit, and hope of glory; as, on the contrary, sense of God's revenging wrath, horror of conscience, and a fearful expectation of judgment, are to the wicked the beginning of their torments which they shall endure after death.
before.right: Believers enjoy God's love, peace, joy, and hope as firstfruits of glory; the wicked, God's wrath and fear of judgment.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Romans 6:23 calls death the wages of sin, Hebrews 9:27 says man is appointed to die once, and Romans 5:12 says death passed to all men because all sinned.

before.question: Shall all men die?
before.answer: Death being threatened as the wages of sin, it is appointed unto all men once to die; for that all have sinned.
before.right: Death as the wages of sin is appointed unto all men once, for all have sinned

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Death is the last enemy destroyed (1 Cor 15:26), and in death the sting is taken away by Christ's victory (1 Cor 15:55-57). The righteous are taken from evil into peace (Isa 57:1-2) and depart to be with Christ (Phil 1:23).

before.question: Death, being the wages of sin, why are not the righteous delivered from death, seeing all their sins are forgiven in Christ?
before.answer: The righteous shall be delivered from death itself at the last day, and even in death are delivered from the sting and curse of it; so that, although they die, yet it is out of God's love, to free them perfectly from sin and misery, and to make them capable of further communion with Christ in glory, which they then enter upon.
before.right: Righteous are freed from death's sting through God's love which frees them from sin and unites them with Christ in glory.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Acts 24:15 gives a resurrection of both righteous and wicked; 1 Corinthians 15:51-52 says the living are changed in an instant; John 5:28-29 says those in graves come out; 1 Corinthians 15:42-44 and Philippians 3:21 describe the glorified body.

before.question: What are we to believe concerning the resurrection?
before.answer: We are to believe, that at the last day there shall be a general resurrection of the dead, both of the just and unjust: when they that are then found alive shall in a moment be changed; and the selfsame bodies of the dead which were laid in the grave, being then again united to their souls forever, shall be raised up by the power of Christ. The bodies of the just, by the Spirit of Christ, and by virtue of his resurrection as their head, shall be raised in power, spiritual, incorruptible, and made like to his glorious body; and the bodies of the wicked shall be raised up in dishonor by him, as an offended judge.
before.right: General resurrection of just and unjust; living changed in moment; bodies raised and united to souls; just in power and incorruption

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: John 5:28-29 places the resurrection of the dead alongside judgment; Jude 1:6 speaks of angels kept for judgment; Matthew 24:36, 44 and Luke 21:36 say the day is unknown, so watch and be ready.

before.question: What shall immediately follow after the resurrection?
before.answer: Immediately after the resurrection shall follow the general and final judgment of angels and men; the day and hour whereof no man knows, that all may watch and pray, and be ever ready for the coming of the Lord.
before.right: General and final judgment of angels and men; day and hour unknown, so all watch and pray

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: The righteous are caught up to meet the Lord, set at his right hand, acknowledged, given eternal life, made holy, joined by the saints and angels, and given rest and joy in God's presence.

before.question: What shall be done to the righteous at the day of judgment?
before.answer: At the day of judgment, the righteous, being caught up to Christ in the clouds, shall be set on his right, and there openly acknowledged and acquitted, shall join with him in the judging of reprobate angels and men, and shall be received into heaven, where they shall be fully and forever freed from all sin and misery; filled with inconceivable joys, made perfectly holy and happy both in body and soul, in the company of innumerable saints and holy angels, but especially in the immediate vision and fruition of God the Father, of our Lord Jesus Christ, and of the Holy Spirit, to all eternity. And this is the perfect and full communion, which the members of the invisible church shall enjoy with Christ in glory, at the resurrection and day of judgment.
before.right: Righteous caught to Christ's right, acquitted, judge reprobates, received to heaven, perfectly holy in God's presence eternally

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Moses declares God's statutes and ordinances to Israel (Deut 5:1), life comes to those who do them (Gal 3:12), a curse on those who break them (Gal 3:10), and holiness reaches soul and body (1 Thess 5:23) all the days of life (Luke 1:75).

before.question: What is the moral law?
before.answer: The moral law is the declaration of the will of God to mankind, directing and binding everyone to personal, perfect, and perpetual conformity and obedience thereunto, in the frame and disposition of the whole man, soul and body, and in performance of all those duties of holiness and righteousness which he oweth to God and man: promising life upon the fulfilling, and threatening death upon the breach of it.
before.right: God's declaration of will directing to personal, perfect, perpetual conformity and obedience in whole man, promising life and threatening death

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Galatians 2:16 and Romans 3:20 show no one is justified by the law; 1 Timothy 1:8-9 says the law is good when used legitimately, and is laid down for the lawless. Romans 8:4 shows its righteous standard is fulfilled in believers.

before.question: Is there any use of the moral law to man since the fall?
before.answer: Although no man, since the fall, can attain to righteousness and life by the moral law; yet there is great use thereof, as well common to all men, as peculiar either to the unregenerate, or the regenerate.
before.right: No man can attain righteousness by law since fall, yet the law has great use for all and unregenerate and regenerate

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: God's holiness and will set the standard of duty (Lev 11:44). The law brings awareness of sin (Rom 3:20), all have fallen short (Rom 3:23), and the law cannot give life, so all are confined by sin and need faith in Christ (Gal 3:21-22).

before.question: Of what use is the moral law to all men?
before.answer: The moral law is of use to all men, to inform them of the holy nature and will of God, and of their duty, binding them to walk accordingly; to convince them of their disability to keep it, and of the sinful pollution of their nature, hearts, and lives; to humble them in the sense of their sin and misery, and thereby help them to a clearer sight of the need they have of Christ, and of the perfection of his obedience.
before.right: Informs of God's will and duty, convinces of sin and inability, humbles us, and shows our need of Christ

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: The law leads people to Christ (Gal 3:24), its accusing conscience (Rom 2:15), leaves men without excuse (Rom 1:20), and those who rely on works lie under its curse (Gal 3:10).

before.question: What particular use is there of the moral law to unregenerate men?
before.answer: The moral law is of use to unregenerate men, to awaken their consciences to flee from wrath to come, and to drive them to Christ; or, upon their continuance in the estate and way of sin, to leave them inexcusable, and under the curse thereof.
before.right: Awakens consciences to flee wrath and drive to Christ; or if sin continues, leaves inexcusable and under curse

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: Believers are not under law but under grace (Rom 6:14), Christ bore the law's curse for us (Gal 3:13), the law's standard is fulfilled in us (Rom 8:3-4), and Christ redeemed us to be zealous for good works (Titus 2:14).

before.question: What special use is there of the moral law to the regenerate?
before.answer: Although the regenerate, who believe in Christ, are delivered from the moral law as a covenant of works, so that they are neither justified nor condemned by it, it still has a special use for them: to show them how much they owe to Christ for fulfilling the law and bearing its curse in their place and for their good, and so to move them to greater thankfulness and to a more careful effort to obey it as the rule of their life.
before.right: Regenerate delivered from law as covenant; law shows how bound to Christ for fulfilling it and enduring curse, provoking thankfulness

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms:westmins.note: The shown verses teach the law is perfect (Ps 19:7; James 2:10), spiritual and reaching inward sins (Rom 7:14; Matt 5:21-28), and that a sin's contrary duty is required (Eph 4:28; Lev 19:17). Rule 5 is not directly shown.

before.question: What rules are to be observed for the right understanding of the ten commandments?
before.answer: For the right understanding of the ten commandments, these rules are to be observed: 1. That the law is perfect, and binds everyone to full conformity in the whole man to its righteousness, and to entire obedience forever; so as to require the utmost perfection of every duty, and to forbid the least degree of every sin. 2. That it is spiritual, and so reaches the understanding, will, affections, and all other powers of the soul, as well as words, works, and gestures. 3. That one and the same thing, in different respects, is required or forbidden in several commandments. 4. That as, where a duty is commanded, the contrary sin is forbidden; and where a sin is forbidden, the contrary duty is commanded: so, where a promise is given, the contrary warning is included; and where a warning is given, the contrary promise is included. 5. That what God forbids is never to be done; what He commands is always our duty; yet not every particular duty is to be done at all times. 6. That under one sin or duty, all of the same kind are forbidden or commanded, together with all the causes, means, occasions, and appearances of it, and temptations to it. 7.
